## Editor's Introduction

<!-- p. 1 -->

The *Account of the Life of David Brainerd* deserves close attention, for it reveals a side of colonial life that is often overlooked. Long confined to the libraries of rare book rooms and missionary societies, it is not now widely read, yet it speaks as directly to the issues of its day as do Edwards' other works. It has been reprinted more often than has any other Edwards work. The text, to be sure, is largely Brainerd's, with editorial comments distributed throughout, but the volume as Edwards conceived it belongs to him. It belongs, moreover, to the period of the Great Awakening, when in the third and fourth decades of the eighteenth century religious enthusiasm swept the colonial frontier.

Because Brainerd had been active during the Awakening, Edwards looked to him for an example of the good rather than the excessive "effects" of experimental religion. Indeed, it has been suggested that Edwards actually exploited Brainerd's life in order to distinguish for the times the genuine "New Birth" from enthusiasm.[^003-note1] What should be said, however, is that Edwards for the most part let the author speak for himself, and that Brainerd described at length what proved to be an arduous task. More than that, Brainerd questioned at times his qualifications for the missionary life: there are hints throughout the diary that his calling may not have been true, that he had taken upon himself (for the wrong reasons) a job for which he was not properly fit. He carried on, to be sure, out of a strong sense of duty, but his joyless determination to persevere set the tone of the text.

Brainerd firmly believed, nevertheless, in the mission task. Like Edwards, he held that contact with the Indians was a means by which the glory of the church might be spread. Missions, both for Brainerd as author and for Edwards as editor, were a major device by which to bring about the millennium: and when Edwards published his account of Brainerd's life in 1749, these millennial

<!-- p. 2 -->

expectations were firmly linked to missionary zeal.[^003-note2] When the heathen are converted, it was held, Indians shall become divines and all nations shall be one. Although Brainerd's personal struggles may be more evident in the diary than his aspirations for the kingdom of God among the Indians, these aspirations were significant—giving Edwards ample reason for editing the text.

For four years, from 1743 to 1747, Brainerd carried out his solitary task: on the western border of Massachusetts, in eastern New York, and throughout the region known as the Forks of the Delaware. In addition, he founded a mission in central New Jersey, where in 1745, he met with his greatest success. But the reader should not expect to find romance. One looks in vain for an heroic frontiersman, a noble sachem, or an inspired woodland scene. The settlers, mainly Scots-Irish, are depicted as slovenly and mean. The Indians are resentful, hounded by the Dutch, and the forest is a "howling wilderness" greatly to be feared. There is nothing here of the forest that James Fenimore Cooper later described—nothing to suggest that the eighteenth-century wilderness might be a breeding ground of heroism and wisdom. Brainerd disliked the wild because he hated the discomforts that living in the woods entailed. When his horse broke a leg, he had immediately to kill it, leaving himself stranded. Indeed, he spent much of his time miles from any settlement, and as skilled as he was in following the woodland path, he lived in fear that when next he lost his way he might not be able to survive. Plagued by disease, riding thousands of miles on horseback, he persevered until the end when, on October 9, 1747, he died in Edwards' house.

He had not at any time led a happy life; he was prone to extreme moods of temperament, the blackest of these brought on by exposure to Indian life. Most frustrating of all, his converts were inclined to die. Indeed, the greatest number of Indian victims of disease were always to be found among those who had been civilized. (Brainerd's converts, of course, were thoroughly exposed to the tuberculosis from which he eventually died.) Finally, although historians over the years have made every effort to shape Brainerd into the foremost missionary of his times, his achievement in the field was slight; he made relatively few converts along the way.

<!-- p. 3 -->

What should be said, moreover, is that Brainerd's failure in the field has rarely been stressed. Edwards skirted the issue. His *Life of Brainerd* soon became a spiritual classic and a model for missionary histories. In the words of Thomas H. Johnson, it was "the first biography written in America that achieved wide notice abroad as well as at home."[^003-note3] Gideon Hawley, another missionary protégé of Edwards, carried in his saddlebag a copy of the *Life*, to which he referred when unable to stand the strain of another day. "I need, greatly need something more than humane to support me," he wrote in 1753. "I read my Bible and Mr. Brainerd's Life, the only books I brought with me, and from them have a little support."[^003-note4] John Wesley was so impressed that he published a condensed version (1768). "Let every preacher read carefully over the 'Life of David Brainerd,'" he instructed in the handbook of the Methodist ministry. Although Wesley could be critical of Brainerd for "applauding himself and magnifying his own work," his example was upheld. "Find preachers of David Brainerd's spirit," he wrote in his journal (1767), "and nothing can stand before them."[^003-note5]

Francis Asbury (1745–1816), who in 1771 became the first missionary of Methodism to America, later referred to Brainerd as "that model of meekness, moderation, temptation and labor, and self-denial." Still another Methodist, Thomas Coke (1747–1814), founder of missions throughout the world, wrote of Brainerd on coming to America in 1784: "His humility, his self-denial, his perseverence and his flaming zeal for God, are exemplary indeed."[^003-note6] Among those who were inspired by the *Life of Brainerd* actually to become missionaries, the most notable were the Baptist William Carey (1761–1834) and the Anglican Henry Martyn (1781–1812). Carey, one of the first missionaries to India and translator of the Scriptures into numerous languages and dialects, considered the *Life* to be a sacred text. Martyn, equally famous as a translator, first read the *Life* while at Cambridge in 1802.

<!-- p. 4 -->

"I long to be like him," he wrote of Brainerd, and like Brainerd, died of tuberculosis (while serving in India with Carey).[^003-note7] Others of this era who testified to the importance of Brainerd in their lives were Samuel Marsden, missionary to Australia and New Zealand, Robert Morrison, Scottish missionary to China, Samuel John Mills, American missionary to India, and Christian Frederick Schwartz, German missionary to India.[^003-note8]

Most of these figures flourished at the turn of the century, but Brainerd's influence did not end there. Robert McCheyne, who organized missions for the Church of Scotland, wrote of Brainerd in 1832: "Most wonderful man! What conflicts, what depressions, desertions, strength, advancement, victories, within thy torn bosom! … Tonight more set upon missionary enterprise than ever."[^003-note9] And David Livingston, famous in Africa, was also inspired by Brainerd,[^003-note10] as was John Wilson in Western India,[^003-note11] Andrew Murry in South Africa,[^003-note12] and Sheldon Jackson in Alaska.[^003-note13] Indeed, it has been said that "David Brainerd dead" more greatly influenced the missionary cause than did "David Brainerd alive."[^003-note14] It has also been said that to the twentieth-century mind Brainerd is no longer the saintly example of the ideal missionary but "an example of the exact opposite."[^003-note15] Yet in 1956 the missionary Jim Elliot, inspired by Brainerd, flew with four companions to the Auca Indians in South America.[^003-note16] "Confession of pride—suggested by David Brainerd's Diary yesterday—must become an hourly thing with me," Elliot wrote shortly before he died.[^003-note17] Elliot had admired Brainerd's courage; but in the jungles of Ecuador he faced a tribe far more hostile than any that Brainerd had met—even in the upper reaches of the Susquehanna.[^003-note18]

<!-- p. 5 -->

### 1. The Place of the Diary in Edwards' Life and Thought

The major works that Edwards published between 1736 and 1746 were efforts to describe the revivals and to define the religious life. His *Life of Brainerd* should be grouped with these. It stands, in 1749, as a sequel to his earlier revival writings. It is, moreover, one of the most important of these writings, mainly because it concentrates upon the religious faith of one man. In no other work does Edwards confront the spiritual life with such an abundance of concrete evidence so close at hand. In no other work is the reader made so vividly aware of Edwards' personal response to the events of the time. As Perry Miller has said, Edwards interpreted Brainerd "as a rebuke both to enthusiasts and to Arminians."[^003-note19] The enthusiasts, who assumed that God already loved them and that his love would descend in a moment of direct revelation, could not point to one example of perseverence in religion such as Brainerd displayed. The Arminians, who emphasized moral behavior as the true sign of a man's spiritual state, could not give one example of their doctrine's having brought about such a moral alteration as that which occurred in Brainerd. The voice that spoke from the diary both condemned the excesses of the Awakening and challenged Arminianism, which Edwards now feared was the greater danger to New England spiritual life.

#### Revival Writings

The diary, above all, allowed Edwards to present "case histories." He had used case histories in *A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God* (1736). Later, in *The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God* (1741), he had described in religious experience what he considered to be valid, sorting out the false from the true. *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival of Religion in New England* (1742) allowed him once again to concentrate on case histories, and in *A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections* (1746), he went on to describe in detail the nature and theory of the religious life. But in none of these works had he anything like the bulk of raw material that Brainerd had left behind. In none had he Brainerd's example on which to draw, for the diary revealed

<!-- p. 6 -->

a perfect example of authentic spirituality, namely Brainerd himself. What is more, Brainerd's saga revealed the thoughts of one who was not an "idle spectator" but who had experienced the Awakening at close quarters and had observed the "extraordinary effects and unusual appearances of that day."[^003-note20]

Brainerd, of course, had described in his diary numerous case histories, namely those of his own converts. It would seem, furthermore, that he had judged these cases by Edwards' rules, which he found in *The Distinguishing Marks*. Although Brainerd does not mention this volume, we find under *Further Remains* (III) "The distinguishing marks of a true Christian, taken from one of my old manuscripts." He clearly knew the signs of faith—both positive and negative—that Edwards had defined. The first edition of *The Distinguishing Marks* (1741), the London edition of 1742, or one of the two Scottish editions of that year, had undoubtedly come his way. Moreover, he had listened to the commencement address (September 10, 1741) from which the printed text was taken.

Indeed, the influence of Edwards' works has always to be taken into account. We know that Brainerd read the *Affections* (Letter No. 10), but he must have read the earlier works as well. Certain notions that appear in the diary could only have come from Edwards. More than that, one senses on Brainerd's part an attempt to parrot his mentor. He conformed, with certain exceptions, to Edwards' rules.

Edwards, in *The Distinguishing Marks*, had allowed for spiritual effects of "the most extraordinary kind," such as "throwing the body into great agonies and extorting great outcries." "That persons have many impressions on their imaginations," he wrote, "don't prove that they have nothing else."[^003-note21] And Brainerd, like Edwards, felt frequently the need to show that "ecstasy" and the true work of the Spirit can go together. Brainerd, to be sure, held that sinners responded best to "the tender and melting invitation of the Gospel, when there was not a word of terror spoken to them"; but the results were still chaotic. On one occasion, we are told, many were so affected that "some few could neither go nor stand, but lay flat on the ground, as if pierced at heart, crying

<!-- p. 7 -->

incessantly for mercy."[^003-note22] Of a woman who had suffered "agony in seeking after Christ," he wrote: "I had never seen such an appearance of ecstasy and humility meeting in any one person in all my life before."[^003-note23] In short, ecstasy was not necessarily enthusiasm, which was the main point that Edwards had made in *The Distinguishing Marks*.

By enthusiasm, needless to say, Brainerd meant antinomianism, which he greatly feared. Although few revivalists had gone so far as to embrace antinomian doctrine, their enthusiasm and zeal had led to similar concepts—to the notion of conversion as a sudden flash: and for this reason Brainerd was careful to distinguish between "ecstasy" and instantaneous conversion. But of greatest interest to Edwards was Brainerd's own conversion. As the Preface to the diary reveals, when Edwards set aside time to examine Brainerd's papers, he was still disturbed by revivalist preaching that had stressed instantaneous conversion, so that Brainerd's account served a useful purpose indeed. Brainerd's conversion, with which the diary begins, was as useful to Edwards as that of Sarah Pierrepont Edwards had been earlier. In *Some Thoughts* her conversion had served as a model.

In *Some Thoughts*, however, Edwards had not informed the reader that it was Sarah, his wife, whose firsthand account he had transcribed. She is referred to throughout as "the person"; her identity and sex are never disclosed, for by rendering her anonymous and sexless Edwards could stress the experiences themselves. He could show, as C. C. Goen has observed, that "in none of her experiences were there any impulses, revelations, superstitions, antinomian delusions, or melancholic seizures." Goen has remarked as well that "her testimony became the final case history that Edwards could set before the world to authenticate the revival":[^003-note24] and in a sense, of course, this remark is true. When Edwards published *Some Thoughts*, he had no idea that Brainerd's papers would one day fall into his hands. But when they did, he had additional case histories with which to "authenticate the revival" and none that need be disguised. Sarah's case had served Edwards well in 1742, but with Brainerd's text he could do more. He could include in his *Life of Brainerd* numerous case histories—

<!-- p. 8 -->

some reported in detail. In addition, because Brainerd had frequently reviewed the process of his own conversion, hoping that repeated experiences of contrition and humiliation would restore his original sense of the Spirit's presence, Edwards had an expanded text with which to work. "I greatly dreaded the loss of convictions, and returning back to a state of carnal security, and to my former insensibility of impending wrath," Brainerd wrote. The most that he could hope for, however, was a "divine temper, whereby the soul exhalts God and treads itself in the dust."[^003-note25] Like other Puritan saints, both before and after his time, he could never be sure that his spiritual state was secure.

Brainerd, like Sarah Edwards, had known "legal terrors," or contrition and humiliation. No sudden illumination had transformed him. He was then made aware that "faith alone was the condition of salvation," that he could do nothing to earn it: he must be willing to be damned. When finally overcome by grace, "unspeakable glory" opened to his soul, but that glory he carefully defined: "I don't mean any external brightness, for I saw no such thing, nor do I intend any imagination of a body of light … or anything of that nature; but it was a new inward apprehension or view that I had of God."[^003-note26] It was, moreover, an experience of conversion that directly contravened the antinomian stance.

Of Brainerd's conversion, which resembled Sarah's to a remarkable degree, Edwards wrote that the young man had not been excited by "strong and lively images formed in his imagination."[^003-note27] Of Sarah's conversion Edwards had said: "Now if such things are enthusiasm, and the fruits of a distempered mind, let my brain be evermore possessed of that happy distemper."[^003-note28] He had also observed of Sarah that she had "formerly in lower degrees of grace, been subject to unsteadiness, and many ups and downs, in the frame of mind; the mind being under great disadvantages, through a vapory habit of body, and often subject to melancholy, and at times almost overborne with it, it having been so even from early youth."[^003-note29] There were, in short, striking similarities between the two cases; as spiritual biography the *Life of Brainerd* carried on where Edwards had earlier left off.

<!-- p. 9 -->

Edwards, of course, looked to Brainerd's converts as well. In April of 1743, at Kaunaumeek, Brainerd was convinced that the Indians could not be converted. "Feared," he wrote, "that nothing would ever be done for them to any happy effect." "To an eye of reason," he shortly afterwards remarked, "everything that respects the conversion of the heathen is as dark as midnight."[^003-note30] Although he preached at frequent intervals, it was not until June of 1745 that he was able to record a first genuine success, reporting that numerous persons were brought under "great concern for their souls" and "shed many tears." Throughout the summer he continued to have successes, recording in August that some who listened were caused "to cry out in anguish of soul." But why he suddenly gained these triumphs is not clear, for his method and doctrine remained unchanged. Nothing in the diary suggests that he altered his approach. "I spoke not a word of terror," wrote Brainerd, "but on the contrary, set before them the … all-sufficiency of Christ's merits."[^003-note31] Unlike some, he did not use "harangues of terror." He did, however, preach the law as well as the Gospel. The "Spirit of bondage," he maintained, must precede the "Spirit of adoption," otherwise the soul cannot come to Christ. Still, his emphasis on Gospel invitation not only contradicted critics of revival preaching but also fitted in with Edwards' reaction against the extremes of Whitefield and other early revival preachers. Like most later revivalists, Brainerd wanted to reach men's hearts, not terrify them. The "anguished" become distressed, he declared, not because they are subject to the "terrors of hell" but because they cannot gain the "happiness of the godly."[^003-note32]

It should be stressed in this regard that Brainerd, unlike Edwards, emphasized the nature of conversion, or the process by which the "godly" achieved their end. Where Edwards assumed that true piety may be determined "without entering into any controversies about the nature of conversion," and that only "the more essential things which belong to it ought to be professed,"[^003-note33] Brainerd demanded a close relation of "beginnings," or "preparatory work." In keeping with Eliot and other first-generation

<!-- p. 10 -->

Puritan divines, Brainerd focused upon a process leading toward conversion and possible assurance of election, while Edwards looked upon conversion as one of the many "signs" of election. But Edwards did not make an issue of the matter, though he may have been tempted to do so, for many of Brainerd's charges did bog down in "preparatory work." Conviction of sin at times led only to "anguish" and "distress." The convicted saw no "safety" in preparation, wrote Brainerd, "unless they could do something towards saving themselves."[^003-note34]

Although Brainerd saw the danger of his method, he ordinarily claimed that nothing "boisterous" or "unseemly" happened. Of his preaching he wrote: "It produced no boisterous commotions of the passions, but seemed deeply to affect the heart."[^003-note35] In one section of his Public *Journal* he is careful to report "no visionary notions, trances, and imaginations intermixed with those rational convictions of sin."[^003-note36] Edwards, of course, did not wish to present his protégé as faulty in doctrine or method. The missionary had done his job. He had, moreover, described at first hand the spiritual effects of the time. Had Edwards deliberately sought out an epilogue to his revival writings, he could not have done better. Nor could he have chosen a better prologue to his later works.

#### Other Publications

During the summer of 1747, as Brainerd lay dying in the Northampton house, Edwards wrote to the Reverend John Erskine, a Church of Scotland minister, that he was thinking of writing "something particularly and largely on the Arminian controversy." A year later, on August 31, 1748, he again wrote to Erskine: "I have for the present, been diverted from the design I hinted to you, of publishing something against some of the Arminian Tenets, by something else that Divine Providence unexpectedly laid in my way, and seemed to render unavoidable, viz. publishing Mr. Brainerd's Life, of which the enclosed papers of proposals gives some account."[^003-note37] In order to edit the diary, Edwards

<!-- p. 11 -->

had put aside the treatise that would take the Arminians to task, his *Freedom of the Will* (1754). But in his next treatise, *The Doctrine of Original Sin Defended* (1758), he again took the Arminians to task, and this time he appears to have drawn on the diary, for missions—both in America and abroad—are used to give the argument strength.

If natural man is able of his own accord to follow God's will, asked Edwards, how can it be explained that "savages" who have not known saving grace persist in their ways? "What appearances was there, when the Europeans first came hither, of their being recovered, or recovering, in any degree from the grossest ignorance, delusions, and most stupid paganism? And how is it at this day, in those parts of Africa and Asia, into which the light of the Gospel has not penetrated?" Edwards, of course, had found the Mohawks who came to Stockbridge from the interior to be far less manageable than the Housatonics. Heathens who lived where "the light of the Gospel" had not come, he affirmed, showed a "natural stupidity" that condemned them to "worship and trust in idols." "This strong and universally prevalent disposition of mankind to idolatry," Edwards observed, "is a most glaring evidence of the exceeding depravity of human nature." One encounters in the heathen world, he declared, "brutish stupidity," and here he may have drawn on Brainerd's accounts; for Brainerd too had been appalled by the "brutish" nature of the heathen, especially on the Susquehanna. Among contemporary observers, Brainerd had most vividly described "the idolatry of the heathen world" and the transformation of the heathen where "the light of the Gospel" had been spread.[^003-note38]

Edwards, of course, had long been concerned with the missionary's role. In one of a series of sermons written in 1739, he had defined the missionary's task, stressing the importance of the work in America, where Satan had established his rule. Because the American continent had been unknown to Christian nations for many centuries, said Edwards, the devil had those who inhabited this part of the world "secure to himself" and "out of the reach of the light of the Gospel." Here many Indian nations worshipped the devil "from age to age," while the Gospel was confined to the other side of the world. Indeed, Edwards explained, it has been said "that the occasion of the first peopling of America

<!-- p. 12 -->

was this, that the devil, being alarmed and surprised by the wonderful success of the Gospel which there was the first three hundred years after Christ … and seeing the Gospel spread so fast, and fearing that his heathenish kingdom would be wholly overthrown through the world, led away a people from the other continent into America, that they might be quite out of the reach of the Gospel, that here he might quietly possess them, and reign over them as their god." Whether or not this traditional account is true, Edwards remarked, there can be no doubt that the devil did assert his "dominion" over the Indians for many years. But now, at last, that has changed: "God has sent the Gospel into these parts of the world, and now the Christian church is set up here in New England, and in other parts of America, where before had been nothing but the grossest heathenish darkness."[^003-note39]

Edwards was willing to admit, nevertheless, that there was much to be done. "And however small the propagation of the Gospel among the heathen here in America has been hitherto," he continued, "yet I think we may well look upon the discovery of so great a part of the world as America, and the bringing of the Gospel into it, as one thing by which divine Providence is preparing the way for the future glorious times of the church; when Satan's kingdom shall be overthrown … throughout the whole habitable globe, on every side, and on all its continents." Moreover, when those times come, he maintained, "then doubtless the Gospel, which is already brought over into America, shall have glorious success, and all the inhabitants of this new discovered world, shall become subjects of the kingdom of Christ, as well as all the other ends of the earth."[^003-note40]

These remarks, which anticipate Brainerd's task, Edwards hoped to revise as part of his "great work," *A History of the Work of Redemption*, but he died before the revisions could be made. The 1739 "rough draft" that Jonathan Edwards, Jr., sent to Scotland for publication in 1774 became the printed text. However, in another posthumously printed work, *The Nature of True Virtue*, Edwards could incorporate Brainerd's example into the finished draft.

Edwards, in the spring of 1755, had started work on this treatise,

<!-- p. 13 -->

which was published in 1765, seven years after he died: and though Brainerd is not mentioned in the text, he is clearly there. More than that, the extent to which he provides for Edwards the model of the true saint must be seriously considered; for Edwards in this work identified true sainthood with total commitment to making the condition of mankind as "excellent" or "beautiful" as God had intended. Benevolence toward "some particular persons or private systems," he wrote in *True Virtue*, is not enough; for "such limited private benevolence, not arising from, nor being subordinate to benevolence to being in general, cannot have the nature of true virtue."[^003-note41] True spirituality, said Edwards, is not simply the experience of grace, but strenuous exertion directed toward correcting the errors of the world: and in Brainerd he had the example of a man who had strained himself to the point of death.

Edwards, of course, was not so much interested in the young man's mission to the Indians as in his commitment to a holy cause—his willingness to abandon all comfort for the sake of redeeming society. It was Brainerd's benevolence to being in general, not his benevolence to the Indians, that finally mattered; for the mission to the Indians was merely an example of what could be done on a larger scale for all God's people in America. Brainerd's work in this regard prepared the way for promoting God's historical design. If all men imitated Brainerd, they too could help bring about a great and universal benevolence for all mankind. Brainerd had gone into the world and had practiced true virtue at great personal cost. He had suffered for the sake of Christian practice; he had put his faith to the test. By example and deed he had nullified the rationalist, Arminian stance.

It is in this sense, above all, that Brainerd looms as the phantom figure in the text. While the Arminians held that morality is based upon reason and sound judgment, Brainerd considered virtue possible only in the form of acts that flow spontaneously from the indwelling spirit of grace. While the Arminians were inclined to feel that it was not necessary to do anything other than bring reason and judgment to bear on questions of right and wrong, Brainerd held it his duty to fulfill the law of love and to serve his fellow man. This compulsion to serve, this sense of duty,

<!-- p. 14 -->

is what Edwards so greatly admired in the man. The will gained in faith, Edwards maintained, commands an active life, and he saw Brainerd as a man grasped by faith—the whole man, all his faculties—and willing to trust to the Word and to risk acting upon its commands under all conditions. It is not enough simply to allow that the Word is true, Edwards held; belief in the Word must be followed by meaningful acts. If the act that is willed is not performed, then that act is not really willed.

Brainerd knew that at any time he could associate himself with a settled congregation in a comfortable town, but his sense of duty confined him to the lowest of the social order—to the Indians and poor whites. His mission was to the lowest stratum of society. As much as he longed for a settled community, he seemed to know that the closer one got to comfort, the closer one got to Arminianism, to the rationalism that characterized civilized society: and for this reason Edwards praised his stand. In spite of recurring "melancholy," or extreme states of mental depression, Brainerd personified for Edwards *the* ethical man. He personified true virtue because he carried out in deeds what he had willed in his heart; his acts of Christian practice were the clearest evidence of his faith.

#### Communion Controversy

When in 1748 Edwards began to edit Brainerd's diary, he was fully engaged in defending himself against his own parishioners, who for a number of years had taken issue with his stand on communion. Until 1744 Edwards had made no sharp distinction between the converted and the unconverted in administering the Lord's Supper. He had followed the practice of his grandfather, Solomon Stoddard, who had refused to distinguish the regenerate from the unregenerate and had offered "open communion." But Edwards had not been happy with the practice, which departed from that of the founders, and so had demanded a profession of faith from all wishing access to the Supper and full standing in the church. None, however, applied. For four years there were no applicants at all. Then in December of 1748, while Edwards was at work on the Brainerd papers, a candidate applied but refused to offer a profession and was turned down. The following spring a young girl, Mary Hulbert, was about to offer a profession but was frightened out of it, with the result that the church then voted to suspend communion altogether. Toward the

<!-- p. 15 -->

end of 1749, shortly after the *Life of Brainerd* had been published, Edwards wrote to Joseph Bellamy: "All that I do and say is watched by the multitude around me with the utmost strictness … my words and actions are represented in dark colors."[^003-note42] By June of 1750 he had been voted out. The ordeal was at an end.

These events, which surround the editing of the diary, cannot be ignored. Although Edwards never once transcribed a conversation with Brainerd, any connection between the communion controversy and Brainerd's example in the diary ought to be considered; for the principles that Edwards upheld, Brainerd had applied in New Jersey and on the Pennsylvania frontier. Brainerd, as the diary shows, did not immediately baptize and admit to the Supper those whom he converted but waited weeks and even months while he observed the "fruits" of the Spirit. He withheld baptism and communion until he had reason to hope that candidates were "truly religious."[^003-note43] Indeed, Brainerd was as cautious as Edwards when it came to matters of judgment. "I am far from thinking that every appearance and particular instance of affection that has been among us has been truly genuine, and purely from a divine influence," Brainerd wrote. "I am sensible of the contrary. And I doubt not, but that there has been some corrupt mixtures, some chaff as well as wheat, especially since religious concern became so common and prevalent here" (March 22, 1746).[^003-note44] For Edwards, of course, the problem was somewhat different. Northampton then endured a "dead" time in religion; the tone had been set by nominal Christians, baptized at birth, who refused to profess their faith for full standing in the church. As opposed to Brainerd, who in 1745 was sifting the wheat from the chaff, Edwards had no harvest at all.

Still, on matters of discipline, Brainerd and Edwards were one. Eliot too had withheld all rites until the "fruits" of the spirit had been observed. But Brainerd, if following Eliot, was also supporting Edwards. More than that, he was transporting the ideology of the Northampton pulpit into the wilderness. Brainerd, it might be argued, had found in Edwards a surrogate father whose notions of discipline so profoundly influenced his own that

<!-- p. 16 -->

he became—in conscious imitation—a spokesman for Edwards' views. Therefore, Edwards had only to look to the diary for support.

When in 1749 the *Life of Brainerd* appeared, Edwards published the *Humble Inquiry into the Rules of the Word of God Concerning Qualifications Requisite to a Complete Standing and Full Communion in the Visible Christian Church*. He also took the position that his congregation should read the book and allow him to expound it from the pulpit. Whether or not he meant to support his case with the diary cannot be known, as the request to expound was denied. However, the *Humble Inquiry* and the *Life of Brainerd* were closely linked in Edwards' life.

#### Stockbridge Mission

Although Edwards was dismissed from the Northampton church in 1750, he remained in the town until October, 1751, when he went to Stockbridge as a missionary—to the same remote place where Brainerd had gone in 1743. Now, with no hope of gaining a popular pulpit—when no settled town close at hand dared to invite him—there can be little doubt that Brainerd's example eased the decision to take up the Stockbridge mission. Indeed, once Edwards had reluctantly moved his family to that distant outpost, he took up the cause of the Indians and defended them against exploitation with a zeal that must have been inspired by Brainerd's work. What is more, throughout the French and Indian War (1755–1763) he stayed on the frontier while others fled, and by his presence and devotion to his job kept the Stockbridge Indians from taking up arms. Although he could not keep the Mohawks at the mission, the Housatonics remained, and he must surely at this time have gained from Brainerd's account the courage and strength that allowed him to retain control. But his health suffered dreadfully. Throughout these mission years, which came to a close in the last year of his life, he endured severe fever and much physical pain. Like Brainerd, he filled up pages of notebooks while the fever raged. Like Brainerd, he was in many ways unfitted for the appointment.

In spite of his devotion to the job, Edwards was by temperament disqualified to minister to "savages" in the wilderness. From John Sergeant, who began the mission, these Indians had heard sermons in their own language, directed to their special concerns;

<!-- p. 17 -->

from Edwards they heard old sermons composed at Northampton and spoken in a foreign tongue.[^003-note45] He was unable to master a dialect, either Mohawk, Iroquois, or Housatonic. In keeping with Brainerd's example, he depended upon an interpreter to repeat his words. Moreover, circumstances were against him. When in 1751 he first went to Stockbridge, two years after Sergeant's death, he found a mission that lacked leadership, an Indian population divided against itself, and a settlement of whites (dominated by the Williams family) that worked against him. Unlike Brainerd, who traveled to relatively untouched ground, Edwards took on a mission that had been going for seventeen years. Above all, he had wholly to adjust his pastoral life. At Northampton he had been responsible only to the congregation that he served; now he was responsible to more than one congregation, to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, and to the Boston commissioners, who held the purse. He was also responsible for a school, with a schoolmaster who did not come directly under his control.[^003-note46]

Because the site of the Stockbridge mission had been neither a trading post nor an Indian town, but was simply a spot between two Housatonic villages, Edwards continuously had to deal with a setting that was artificial. In winter the Indians camped near the meetinghouse and attended the school, but in summer they went back to their farms and traded their produce to the Dutch for rum.[^003-note47] As a result, Edwards was required to be far more realistic than was Brainerd with respect to religious experience, and much more concerned with drunkeness and crime. He did not make conversion and baptism the main goal of the missionary life, nor did he regard that life as a saintly occupation. Although he suffered from illness, he guarded his health; he did not relish martyrdom in the name of a selfless cause. Nor did he compete with rivals for heathen souls. His conduct as a missionary differed in many ways from the example set in the *Life*.

Gideon Hawley, who began his career at Stockbridge under Edwards in 1752, has left a record that deserves note.[^003-note48] In taking up Brainerd's cause he also preserved glimpses of Edwards' life.

<!-- p. 18 -->

Starting as a schoolmaster for the Iroquois, Hawley went on to set up in 1754 a mission among the Six Nations, near where Brainerd on the Susquehanna had made an unsuccessful attempt eight years before. Because of his knowledge of dialects, Hawley also acted as an interpreter, and on the eve of the French and Indian War he was highly regarded at diplomatic councils. When war broke out, he was obliged to leave his mission and as chaplain joined the expedition to Crown Point. Later he went to Marshpee, on Cape Cod, where he served as missionary from 1758 until he died, in 1807, in his eightieth year.[^003-note49]

Hawley, unlike Brainerd and Edwards, had a single purpose in life, to be a missionary. Like them, he was in many ways unfitted for the job: he wrote uncompromising letters that show a lack of sympathy with Indian character.[^003-note50] Carrying in his saddlebag a copy of the *Life* (published the year he was graduated from Yale, 1749), he would have abandoned his work were it not for the self-sacrifice and sainthood he was seeking. He tells of return visits to Stockbridge, of being nursed by Edwards through illness, and of leading a life of sanctity in obvious imitation of the *Life*. But he was greatly determined where his missionary model was not. Brainerd, who could never gain the colleague he desired, finally had to give the idea up. Hawley, early in his career, wrote, June 13, 1753: "I expect … in due time to have a fellow missionary. I shall insist upon it and make it a term of my continuance in the mission."[^003-note51] He was also more cheerful about life. "Through the goodness of God I am in health," he wrote, on returning to Stockbridge, June 1, 1754. "I find my friends too. I spent 12 days very agreeably at Mr. Edwards's."[^003-note52] After a brief trip to Albany, he wrote: "Wednesday July 3rd to Stockbridge, was very much rejoyced to see Mr. Edwards and his family again—where I tarried till Friday near night." Here he even had time for a novel: "Monday July 15th——16th. I was at Mr. Edwards's reading *Pamela*." Finally, he was always ready to pitch in when his mentor was indisposed: "Lord's Day 25th I preached for Mr. Edwards, he being sick——to the Indians."[^003-note53]

<!-- p. 19 -->

Of special interest are the contrasts between Hawley's journal and Brainerd's diary as edited by Edwards. (Edwards may have wished that the Brainerd of the unedited diary had been more like the self-acknowledged imitator of the diary.) Hawley could be depressed, but he would quickly recover. Although he complained that he needed "something more than humane" to sustain him, relying upon his Bible and "Mr. Brainerd's Life" for "a little support," he could also report that he was "pleased" with Edwards' sermons and in other respects took genuine delight in the spiritual life.

#### Spiritual Life

On the matter of depression Edwards was uneasy with the example that Brainerd had set, and with the psychological problems that even the edited diary reveals. He disliked the excessive introspection in which Brainerd engaged. Morbid introversion, he believed, endangered one's state of mind and disrupted the spiritual life. At the age of twenty, in his own diary, he had written: "It is a most evil and pernicious practice, in meditations on afflictions, to sit ruminating on the aggravations of the affliction, and reckoning up the evil, dark circumstances thereof, and dwelling long on the dark side: it doubles and trebles the affliction."[^003-note54] And in Brainerd's case self-examination clearly had pulled him down, paralyzed him, and hindered his efforts. Yet the heroic quality of Brainerd lay in this very fault, for in spite of the errors of his ways he still had managed to function as a Christian. Therefore, Edwards felt compelled both to blame him and to praise him at the same time. Brainerd is blamed for the melancholy, which slowed down his activity and affected his health, and he is praised for overcoming it as much as he did.

Edwards, of course, did not mean to say that the saint should cease to struggle against the sin that remains within him. The struggle against sin, the doubt of one's state of grace, must be a part of the saintly life. But the problem has to do with what form this concern should take, and for Edwards it should not reach the point of rendering oneself immobile. Because practice is only a sign of faith, not a source, the saint should be able to trust in God's promises when dissatisfied with holy practice; he need not

<!-- p. 20 -->

fall into despair. Therefore, the issue that Edwards must confront in the diary is whether or not Brainerd *can* trust in God when he is unable to practice, when he is distressed by "misimprovement of time." Edwards concludes, it is safe to say, that Brainerd did in the end maintain that trust; he did not, in despair, entirely give up hope. He neither moved back to the revivalistic view that the saint should always feel immediately that he is a man of faith, nor did he move out toward Arminian moral conceits, where it is generally assumed that practice, however slight, brings one closer to a state of grace. Because he held to the notion that assurance is a struggle that must be upheld by a hope in the promises and by a trust in God, he gained Edwards' praise, and this in spite of the "clouds" of depression that had plagued his career from the start.

It has earlier been observed that Brainerd in the diary mirrors Edwards' attitudes to the extent that the younger man in his own life—in his exposure to enthusiasm and Arminianism—struggled with powerful forces in conflict at the time. But it should also be recalled that Brainerd, even more than Edwards, was in the midst of things—actually suffering for his views in a way that Edwards did not do until dismissed from his pulpit. What is more, Brainerd spent most of his adult life trying to recover from having made what he considered to be his one grave mistake—that of falling in with the enthusiasts while at Yale. Such an experience Edwards lacked, in that he was always sure of his views and never took a step that he later considered to be a mistake. He devoted his energies to trying to repair the break in the American religious attitude that had caused the uproar around him, and he saw in Brainerd the example of the mended break—the example of a man who had recovered from the disease of enthusiasm to become a saint of sound faith.

It was not, of course, the rationalists alone who needed to be corrected. The rationalists had emphasized morality at the expense of faith, but the enthusiasts had emphasized irresponsible, sterile faith at the expense of Christian practice. Those who during the Great Awakening had taken up the extremist cause and had condemned others for not having known conversion as the enthusiasts understood it, or who had set themselves up as "separatists" more holy than others, were also for Edwards victims of

<!-- p. 21 -->

bad ethics. He therefore praised Brainerd's piety over theirs because it did not consist in "unaccountable flights and vehement pangs" but was more "like the steady lights of heaven; that are constant principles of light, though sometimes hid with clouds."[^003-note55] Indeed, after the brief flirtation with enthusiasm Brainerd never again separated faith from practice. As a missionary, he took the precise step of putting his faith into practice. His affections, now rightly ordered, allowed him to reject the excesses of the revivals, to distinguish between true "heart religion" and hysteria.

In this regard Edwards' interest in editing the diary stemmed from a deep concern with showing his contemporaries that he was not defending the passions of the revival at the expense of intellect. There must always be a firm sense of intellect at work, of affections working with understanding, and his gleanings from the diary were intended to support this stand; for Brainerd ordinarily distinguished between the way his converts behaved and the way those overcome by hysteria expressed themselves. Moreover, Brainerd's whole effort—as Edwards presented him—was to move away from the passions that had led to excesses in his own behavior, and to work toward a true knowledge of the affections.

That effort, however, required great strength. Since throughout the years among the Indians Brainerd was plagued by physical illness and by mental depression, he disliked much of his work and was tempted to accept offers of a pastorate in a settled community. Above all, he disliked himself much of the time and once confessed that he was "the meanest, vilest, most helpless, guilty, ignorant, benighted creature living."[^003-note56] Rarely did he show genuine satisfaction with what he had done, in spite of considerable success toward the end of his career. He frequently questioned the whole enterprise and felt that he was wasting the money of the missionary society that supported him. His loneliness, his sense of failure with the Indians, together with his tendency to pull himself down at every turn, brought on recurring fits of melancholy. He appeared at times to crave death more than he cherished life. Yet when Edwards published the record that Brainerd

<!-- p. 22 -->

had left, he believed that it set before the reader "a remarkable instance of true and eminent Christian piety in heart and practice … most worthy of imitation."[^003-note57] In spite of Brainerd's misery, in spite of his faults, Edwards saw in him a virtuous man who exemplified the spiritual life.

Edwards, to be sure, omitted those parts of the diary that he disliked, substituted his own summary of them, and at times changed Brainerd's wording. But the editing did not disguise the melancholy tone of the text, nor did Edwards always try to disguise it. Brainerd, Edwards admits, was "prone to melancholy and dejection of spirit."[^003-note58] However, the steady and lasting quality of his religious convictions, Edwards believed, should interest the reader. It was Brainerd's experience of religious truths, rather than his personality, that Edwards stressed. Although the story of this missionary's work was dramatic, although the man himself was sick, desperate, and deprived of comforts, Edwards was mainly concerned with the theological example that the diary provides.

Edwards, of course, showed affection for his young friend, giving thanks that in the end Brainerd "should be cast hither to my house, in his last sickness, and should die here";[^003-note59] but on the whole he presented him not as an individual but as a representative figure. Edwards was concerned with the historical events of Brainerd's life, but he did not want these events to seem significant in themselves. Rather, his use of the diary must be seen as part of a larger effort to answer a basic theological question: "What are the distinguishing qualifications of those that are in favor with God, and entitled to his eternal rewards?"[^003-note60] This question, said Edwards, had been his main concern ever since he first began the study of divinity. It was a question that Brainerd had also asked, both of himself and of others.

Unlike the diaries of most Puritan divines, Brainerd's was not confined to mere introspection, which for Edwards was its great virtue. Christian practice, in Edwards' scheme, was always to be preferred to that which simply begins and ends in contemplation. Yet the inner life must be there; and Brainerd's diary, although

<!-- p. 23 -->

it described "external behavior," was also a record of the interior life. It revealed, as Edwards said, "what passed in his own heart." But it served still another use. Brainerd had traveled extensively from place to place. He had been able to observe a great variety of people who were affected by the revivals—"people of many different nations, of different educations, manners, and customs."[^003-note61] Moreover, he had gone out among these people, Indians and whites alike, and had brought back firsthand information that gave broad factual support to Edwards' stand. But in one respect at least the two could not have differed more. Although Edwards nowhere remarks upon it, Brainerd's response to nature could not have been more different from his own.

Brainerd in this regard was deeply ingrained in the Puritan mold, while Edwards was not. Influenced by the so-called "nature enthusiasts" of the Enlightenment, Edwards gave to nature a mystical quality that is not characteristic of the Puritan. Where Edwards saw mountains and waste places as the setting for divine disclosure, Brainerd saw only a "howling desert." Where Edwards could take spiritual delight "in the sun, moon, and stars; in the clouds, and blue sky; in the grass, flowers, trees,"[^003-note62] Brainerd never mentioned natural beauty. In contrast to Edwards' joy in summer is Brainerd's fear of winter. But while Brainerd's situation was unusual (having to survive under harsh circumstances), his attitude toward nature was not; for the Puritan, in general, failed to respond to natural beauty. "He did not attack the desire for beauty as such," writes M. M. Knappen of the traditional Puritan divine, "but in his diary he never mentioned an attractive landscape or sunset."[^003-note63] Nor did Brainerd in his.

On this issue, however, Edwards let Brainerd have his way. The detachment from natural beauty is never criticized; it is simply overlooked. Brainerd had served, after all, as an "instrument" of a great cause. In life he had given his all for "promoting the revival of true religion." In death, through his literary remains, he had become "the instrument of promoting the interest of religion in this world." "He being dead, yet speaketh" (Hebrews 11:14),

<!-- p. 24 -->

Edwards declared. Indeed, the circumstances of Brainerd's death were fortunate, both for posterity and for his biographer. He might have died "in the wilderness, among the savages," Edwards observed, where the diary would surely have perished. At Boston, in his last illness, he would have suppressed his private papers had his friends not dissuaded him. Moreover, had John Brainerd not brought the diary from New Jersey, without being asked to do so, it might never have been published. And had Edwards not been at Brainerd's side to see his "dying behavior" and hear his "dying prayers," none would have recorded his last days.[^003-note64] Unlike most biographers, Edwards had distinct advantages: he had known his subject in life, had witnessed his death, and had access to his papers from the start. He could therefore compile a biography that did more than supply the facts. He could include himself as a witness to the spiritual life.[^003-note65]

Because the *Life of Brainerd* consists of selections from the diary, which in turn are accompanied by Edwards' comments, it does not demand from the reader a trained ability to follow theological subtleties. In addition, the language is confined to narrative prose, although when Edwards discusses Brainerd's sense of perseverance in religion, his style resembles that of the *Affections*.[^003-note66] But it was the biographer's intention, for the most part, to allow his subject to speak for himself. Although Edwards took great liberties with Brainerd, altering words and deleting whole passages, the diary provides the bulk of the printed text.

### 2. Historical Background

Even though the Massachusetts charter had charged the governor and company to win the natives to the Christian cause, John Winthrop feared that "Papists" and Anglicans had met with greater success than had the Puritans.[^003-note67] Certainly, French Catholics in Canada and Anglicans in the English colonies beyond Massachusetts had brought impressive numbers under their sway. But what the Puritan required of the Indian was far more demanding than

<!-- p. 25 -->

what the Catholic or Anglican asked, and these requirements remained in Brainerd's time: not mere attendance at services, nor declarations of allegiances, but full church membership. Exposure to Christian habits had always to be followed by conversion, otherwise none could be admitted to communion. Moreover, the conversion experience, which was beyond the ken even of most English immigrants, had also to be based on a sound doctrinal stance.[^003-note68]

At first it had been thought that the Indian should be civilized before he was converted. James Hopkins, in the early period of settlement, had written from England to John Winthrop: "If you can first civil the natives, and then bring some of them to know God … you shall have cause to rejoice."[^003-note69] But by Brainerd's time the earlier Puritan belief in the use of civilization as a means of conversion had almost vanished. Now conversion took precedence over civilizing. Indians were to be converted not under the influence of civilization, but on the raw frontier, where Brainerd stressed "experimental religion" as his main concern. Another missionary of the time, Charles Beatty, argued that Indians must first be converted before they are civilized, "for they hate civilization and Christianity equally and must be convinced of the misery of their spiritual state before they can realize the misery of their civil state."[^003-note70]

Some American Indians, to be sure, had been willing from the earliest days to listen to the Christian message, but many had not. Certain aspects of the new religion were not appealing, such as kneeling, the lack of dancing, and the English clothes thought proper for a Christian life. Much in Christian doctrine was profoundly strange, if not repellent, to them, for the Indians of North America had never before considered that man was born into a sinful condition and in need of redemption. To them, all nature was good, and man had been given his place in nature's scheme. Mankind, of course, had always to confront ills such as death, disease, and witchcraft, but these had not come through his fault; they were the result of chance or mischief conjured up by some

<!-- p. 26 -->

primal being. All Indians in North America, furthermore, relied on some person who was supremely fitted to deal with the supernatural—the medicine man, or powwow—and against this formidable figure the missionaries had always to contend (usually in vain) from the first.[^003-note71] Brainerd, as we shall see, was routed by the powwows on his venture up the Susquehanna in 1745. To the natives of the interior, who were then still untouched by whites, the professionalism of the pulpit and the paid exhorter were distinctly unappealing, unspiritual, and unedifying. Indeed, it was not until the spirit of the red man had been broken and his condition undermined by trade and strong drink that missionaries gained any real hold on him: and even then, in his secret soul, he despised the men who had come to convert him.[^003-note72]

It is not surprising therefore that Brainerd made relatively few converts. Nor is it surprising that he held a view of the red man that had come down from earlier times. John Eliot, the "great apostle" to the Indians, had looked upon his charges as "doleful creatures"—the very ruins of mankind.[^003-note73]

Though Eliot felt obliged to carry on missions, he knew that he had taken on a formidable task, for it was up to him to restore to God a lost Israelite tribe. The Indian, he believed, was a descendant not only of Adam but also of Noah and of Asiatic Tartars who had come to the American continent by way of a land-bridge from Asia.[^003-note74] Because of endless wanderings, the red man had lost sight of God, but through the Word he could still be restored; he could still be rescued from Satan's embrace. Because Eliot had assumed that the Indian's nature was essentially the same as his own, he wanted to recover for the American native the same spiritual purity which he sought to regain for himself. Others of his time felt the same way.

Little, however, had been done before Eliot's time to encourage missionary efforts. At first it was assumed that the natives would embrace the Gospel; therefore, extensive plans for missionary

<!-- p. 27 -->

work had not been drawn up. Although Richard Bourne had from 1626 labored at the Cape, and Thomas Mayhew had by 1650 claimed twenty-two converts at Martha's Vineyard, it was not until Eliot began his labors that solid congregations emerged; for Eliot was first to put the Indians into "towns" and to demand strict qualifications for full communion. Between 1651 and 1674 fourteen "praying towns" were established, Natick being chief among them. Still, in the long run, Eliot's achievement was small. Because of the strict admissions procedures in New England, he was not able to gather a church until 1660. What is more, most Indians in the Bay Colony—encouraged by their powwows—remained bitterly hostile to missionary efforts, with the result that few were converted.[^003-note75] Brainerd found in his own time, of course, that every convert had to face the anger of the powwows, to whom the sachems gave strong support.

The extent of Brainerd's success, then, may be measured against these efforts, which had been carried out by few hands at best. Because the first duty of the Puritan preacher was to his immediate congregation, proselytizing had early been put aside. The number of Indian converts in Massachusetts was higher than elsewhere, owing to the work of Eliot and Mayhew, but in the other colonies little had been done.[^003-note76] It was not, after all, an easy job. If properly done, it meant teaching converts how to read; in every case it meant exposing them to a complex theology and to a drastic change in life, and for this reason, among others, interest in the work gradually waned. By 1676, with the conclusion of King Philip's war, the English view of the Indian had in any case changed. Because the red man in his fury had wrought havoc on the settlements, his place in the order of redemption quickly fell. The once lost Israelite had confirmed his kinship with the Canaanite, and in the New Jerusalem he was not to be embraced.[^003-note77] Indeed, King Philip's war had inflicted such a staggering blow on the Indian mission that by the turn of the century missionary work had severely declined: the war had created both indifference to, and hostility toward, the idea of mission.[^003-note78] Although a new phase

<!-- p. 28 -->

in evangelical work was about to begin, Solomon Stoddard would later raise the question "whether God is not angry with the country for doing so little toward the conversion of the Indians."[^003-note79]

In 1697, Samuel Sewall had made a vigorous effort to restore the red man to his assigned place. As the new century neared, Sewall had gone back to the early writers and had stressed millennial expectations. Missions, he declared, belonged to the glorious age of the church, and that age was now at hand.[^003-note80] In challenging the English settlers to renew missions, he had argued that the New Jerusalem could not be realized in America without the conversion of the Indians. The Israelite origins of the natives, he maintained, could still be proved to be true.[^003-note81]

In addition to Sewall, Increase and Cotton Mather had also joined the cry. Increase complained that in the years since Eliot's death "there had been a signal blast of heaven on ye Indian work"; and Cotton in his turn stressed the eschatological role that missions should play.[^003-note82] But by the turn of the century the natives on the eastern seaboard had all but vanished. What is more, because the colonists feared all aborigines who had been exposed to French Catholic rule, the New England leaders in the first quarter of the new century felt unable to start a mission drive in the west. That situation, however, was soon to change; for the increasing threat of French forces in Canada now brought into being a curious partnership of church, state, and a British society, with the Indians of the Housatonic Valley and the Six Nations, or Iroquois, as its main concern.[^003-note83]

Organized in 1701 and chartered by Queen Anne in 1709, the Society in Scotland for Propagating Christian Knowledge took the initiative in this enterprise, which soon led to the mission work of which Brainerd became a part. There had been throughout the first quarter of the eighteenth century a growing volume of missionary work in Scotland.[^003-note84] After years of activity in the Highlands,

<!-- p. 29 -->

where Roman Catholicism and ignorance were the chief foes, the Society in Scotland had in 1730 turned to America, offering sums to Massachusetts for missionary support. With a bequest from Dr. Daniel Williams for the purpose of sending three missionaries to the "infidels," the Society had commissioned Governor Jonathan Belcher and "other gentlemen of character and influence" to form a Boston board of managers and had assigned to them the sum of £56 as the annual income of the Williams bequest.[^003-note85] To this amount the General Court, in approving the enterprise, had given additional financial support for a period of five years, and each of the three volunteers was sent to a frontier post: Joseph Seccombe to Fort George; Ebenezer Hinsdel to Fort Dummer; and Stephan Parker to Fort Richmond. But because they had gone to military posts, where the Indians came and went, they had not the control that was needed. The Iroquois, moreover, had by then been thoroughly exposed to Jesuits, so that at the end of three years the project had to be stopped. For Brainerd's predecessors, the natives were too much under the influence of the French.[^003-note86]

The next venture of the Society was therefore directed toward the people of Mohegan stock in the Housatonic Valley, and it was to these people that the Boston board, in 1736, sent John Sergeant to found a mission. Sergeant's task, so different from that of the first three appointees, was to establish at Stockbridge an Indian town, and to this mission Brainerd went in 1743 in order to learn the Algonquian tongue.[^003-note87] But of greatest importance for Brainerd was the New York board, or New Jersey board, as it was also called, which the Society had set up in 1740 with Ebenezer Pemberton as chairman. This Middle Colonies board soon had more to do than the Boston board, mainly because of the Indians' decline in New England. Composed of Presbyterians, it continued to make common cause with New England Congregationalists, so that the missionaries sent out were all New Englanders, including Brainerd, his brother John, and Azariah Horton, who went to Long Island Sound.

<!-- p. 30 -->

The mission field, however, was not confined to New Englanders. Congregationalists and Presbyterians may have produced the most prominent figures; but other groups were equally dedicated: there were Anglicans and Quakers, along with Moravians and Baptists of several kinds. Brainerd, it is generally agreed, took part in the last phase of missionary activity in the colonies, which was also the most competitive; for rival missions were well under way by the time he got his start.

As early as 1703 an Anglican mission to the Mohawks had been initiated by the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. Although it was later said that the Anglican missionaries seemed mainly to be concerned with proselytizing among other Christians, Anglicans sent back reports that the rigid doctrines and evangelical excesses of the Dissenters were driving both Indians and whites into the Church of England. Anglicans also claimed baptisms in large numbers, raising hopes at home that the future of the Middle Colonies lay with the National Church.[^003-note88] But Anglican success was due not so much to the missionaries, who were few in number, as to Sir William Johnson, superintendent of Indian Affairs for New York, and to the war chief Thayendanegea, or Joseph Brandt, who after 1746 led the entire Mohawk Nation into the Church of England. Johnson, who at first had cooperated with the New England mission, came to oppose it, partly because of religious differences, but mainly because he wanted the allegiance of the Indians without imposing a radical change on their culture. In short, he wanted them warlike but on the English side, for in taking command of the New York colonial forces in 1748 he was fully prepared to campaign against the French.[^003-note89]

Of far greater concern for Brainerd, however, was the mission of the *Unitas Fratrum*, the Moravian Church. Although Anglican missions were effective, the Moravians appear in the diary as Brainerd's principal rivals, having established themselves in the Middle Colonies shortly before he arrived. Indeed, of all the missionary groups they were by far the most passionate in their concern, and for this reason, among others, they challenged the New England cause. They were the first Protestants in America to declare that the conversion of the heathen was the duty of the

<!-- p. 31 -->

Church as such, apart from colonial policy. They believed, moreover, that they above all others had been chosen to spread the Gospel among the Indians, and to this end taught their children the Mohawk tongue.[^003-note90]

The first Moravian mission had begun in Georgia in 1735 but was abandoned because of popular opposition to the pacifist convictions of the missionaries. In 1740 another venture was made on the New York—Connecticut border but was destroyed by hostile settlers of both colonies. When in 1741 Nicholas Ludwig, Count von Zinzendorf, came to America hoping to unite German Protestants, Moravian prospects improved; for through the evangelist George Whitefield the Count acquired land in the Forks of the Delaware on which the Brethren could settle. Although a plot was made to murder Zinzendorf, he nevertheless prevailed, and in 1742 made several trips in the interest of missions among the Indians:[^003-note91] to the Minnisinks, the Blue Mountains, the Aquanshicola, and the Upper Schuylkill. Before sailing back to Europe in 1743, just as Brainerd first ventured into the Middle Colonies, the Count had held a parley with the Chiefs of the Six Nations, had organized an Indian congregation at Shekomeko, in New York, and in Pennsylvania had helped to found Moravian congregations at Bethlehem, Nazareth, Hebron, Heidelberg, Lancaster, and York.[^003-note92]

The Moravians' religious views, however, were highly offensive to the strict Protestant mind, and when Brainerd went into Pennsylvania he did so partly to counteract the Moravians' effort. Once there, he discovered to his horror how widely their views differed from his own, and in this regard the Moravians proved formidable rivals indeed.

Unlike Brainerd, for whom salvation was a process of guilt and pain, the Moravians stressed joyful love of the divine. Because they held that Christ had atoned for human sin, they felt free to love God without continuous penitence: they did not embark on a personal struggle for conversion and salvation. As opposed to Brainerd, who demanded convincing relations of the conversion experience, the Moravian missionaries were content with a mere profession of faith. Moreover, where Brainerd strictly catechized

<!-- p. 32 -->

his charges, the Brethren rejected "the method of teaching them such matters as they can keep in their head, and learn by rote, to say after one."[^003-note93] Above all, and much to Brainerd's distress, these missionaries greatly stressed the image of Christ on the cross—noting his blood and wounds. But there was little that Brainerd could do, for his rivals had long been determined to triumph in the mission field.

The Moravian Brethren, descendants of a pre-Reformation sect that in 1467 had seceded from the Church of Rome, subscribed to a pietistic theology; because they held that works were essential to the maintenance of grace, they brought a powerful ethical force to the mission field. One formidable Moravian of this time was David Zeisburger, who had immigrated to America in 1738. For over sixty years, from 1745, he lived among red men on the closest possible terms, became a member of an Indian family, and was allowed to move among the Six Nations at will.[^003-note94] In 1749, two years after Brainerd's death, Parliament recognized the Moravian *Unitas Fratrum* as an ancient Protestant Episcopal Church, granting it further concessions in the colonies, and of this development Zeisburger took advantage.[^003-note95]

### 3. Historical Figures

Brainerd's greatest rival, however, had not been Zeisburger but himself. Throughout his mission he was chiefly occupied with thoughts of his pollution and defects in the eyes of infinite purity. He combined anxiety with courage to an extraordinary degree. In no other diary of the time do we have such striking evidence of a man so thoroughly divided against himself. What Brainerd wrote, to be sure, was written in a troubled time; on this point the document is clear. Nevertheless, that it was written by a troubled man must also be taken into account.

Brainerd's emotional experiences, according to one biographer, may have been pathological in origin—especially those which he attributed to a divine agency.[^003-note96] From the age of seven he had

<!-- p. 33 -->

been driven to religious duties with unnatural zeal. Much, indeed, might be blamed on his childhood, which had not been emotionally secure. Although his siblings rallied around him, he lacked the love of his father, who before an early death had been remote and severe. When David reached adolescence his mother died, possibly a victim of the same disease that later killed the son. By the time he entered college, and perhaps earlier, he had been infected with that disease, which made him more than ever prone to morbid moods—moods that were deeply rooted in Brainerd's family life.

#### Family

Brainerd's grandfather, Daniel Brainerd, was an orphan who in about 1649, at the age of eight, had been brought from Essex, England, to Hartford, Connecticut. It is not known why he left home so young, who brought him, or in what vessel he sailed. Until he was twenty-one he lived with a family called Wadsworth, and then in 1662 settled in the town of Haddam, where in time he became the greatest landowner, a commissioner for the General Court, a justice of the peace, and a deacon in the church. His first wife, Hannah Spencer, gave birth over the years to a daughter, Hannah, and seven sons: Daniel, James, Joshua, William, Caleb, Elijah, and Hezekiah. Hezekiah Brainerd, born in 1681, became the father of David and the leading member of the family. According to one descendant, Hezekiah was said to have been a man "of great personal dignity and self-restraint, of rigid notions of parental prerogative and authority, of the strictest puritanical views as to religious ordinances, of unbending integrity as a man and a public officer, and of extreme scrupulousness in his Christian life."[^003-note97] Having been "early called … by divine grace," wrote another descendant, he "gave himself up to the practice of religion," and "used to keep days of private fasting to promote his spiritual welfare."[^003-note98] He was a representative in the General Assembly, Speaker of the House in 1721 and 1722, and a member of the Governor's Council, or Senate, from 1723 until he died in office four years later. Before he died the Legislature had given

<!-- p. 34 -->

him, in gratitude for his service, a farm of three hundred acres in Goshen.

Hezekiah's wife, Dorothy Hobart Mason, had been the widow of Daniel Mason, a grandson of Major John Mason who defeated the Pequot Indians in 1637. Her son, Jeremiah Mason, was two and a half years old when she married Hezekiah Brainerd on October 1, 1707. Her father, Jeremiah Hobart, had been Haddam's first minister. His father, Peter Hobart, was a preacher in England who had settled in Hingham, Massachusetts, and three of Jeremiah's brothers were ministers. Dorothy's maternal grandfather, Samuel Whiting, had been one of the foremost Puritan divines, first at Boston, Lincolnshire, and then at Lynn, Massachusetts, and three of her brothers were ministers. Her maternal grandmother, Elizabeth St. John, was a sister of Oliver St. John, Chief Justice of the Common Pleas under Oliver Cromwell: and so it was that when David Brainerd was born, April 20, 1718, he came into a family with a long ministerial and Puritan tradition on his mother's side.[^003-note99]

David was the sixth child born of his mother's second marriage. The first five children were Hezekiah (born 1708), Dorothy (1710), Nehemiah (1712), Jerusha (1714), and Martha (1716). When David was two years old his brother John was born (1720); Elizabeth was born when he was four (1722), and Israel when he was seven (1725). The house in which the ten children lived had been built by David's grandfather, Daniel, and stood one hundred feet above the west bank of the Connecticut River, between Walkley Hill and Higganum, two miles above Haddam village. It was a well-run house, wherein Scripture reading was daily required. Church attendance was also rigidly enforced, and for this purpose David was taken to the town's new meetinghouse, built in 1721. Shingled, clapboarded, and plastered inside with lime made from oyster shells, this house had pews and galleries, in which David was compelled to sit. Because neighboring Indians had the right to fish and hunt in the countryside, and at times harassed the town, the villagers carried arms on their way to meeting. The congregation, it would seem, was entirely English, but the sight of an Indian must have been a familiar and early one in Brainerd's life. In this provincial place, school was kept at first in a village house; no money for a schoolhouse appears on

<!-- p. 35 -->

the town records before 1728. Whether or not David attended cannot be determined; he may have been taught by the minister, or at home.[^003-note100]

The Brainerd children, it would appear, formed close bonds among themselves; for their parents, as we have seen, did not live long. David was nine when his father died at the age of forty-six. When the mother died five years later David was only fourteen. As a result, he became obsessed with the brevity of life—a theme that pervades the diary throughout. Indeed, he seems never to have fully recovered from these deaths, which left him feeling deserted. It has been said of Brainerd that from childhood he was "terrified by the thought of death," and that as a child he was "highly emotional, unhealthily introspective, over-conscientious, and subject to periods of dark depression."[^003-note101] It has also been said that he was "a thoughtful boy, with a tinge of melancholy, which the loss of his parents and the barrenness and narrowness of his education, according to the views of the day, doubtless intensified." His emotional and spiritual anxieties, we are told, may also be attributed to sheer isolation: "The loneliness of the frontier settlement where he was living also had its effect…. His continual self-examination, his highly sensitive and melancholy temperament and his inherited trait of piety combined to produce in him that highly exalted state in which he saw visions of light, and felt the actual presence of the Invisible."[^003-note102]

When David had to some degree recovered from his mother's death, he began a new life. His sister Jerusha, then eighteen, had married Samuel Spencer of East Haddam. She was David's favorite sister and closest confidante at the time. Edwards says that "a particularly dear affection, and much intimacy in spiritual matters" had "long subsisted" between them.[^003-note103] Indeed, Edwards describes this friendship in much the same way that he later describes the bond that grew between Brainerd and the second Edwards daughter, also named Jerusha, who at seventeen nursed Brainerd in his last days. But whether or not Brainerd was later drawn to Jerusha Edwards because her name and spiritual interests brought back the memory of his sister cannot be known. We

<!-- p. 36 -->

know only that the young orphan, in the spring of 1732, just before his fifteenth birthday, moved to East Haddam, where he lived for four years with his sister and brother-in-law and their first three children. During these years of adolescent life he describes himself as "something sober, and inclined rather to melancholy than the contrary extreme,"[^003-note104] a habit of mind that he would carry with him long after he had left his sister's house.

On his nineteenth birthday, in April of 1737, Brainerd inherited a share of his father's land—a farm at Durham, ten miles west of Haddam. That month he moved to the land, spent the summer working it, and soon found out that the farmer's ways were not what he wanted. What he did want, it appears, was to excel as his older brothers had done. Hezekiah had in 1734 succeeded his father as Representative to the General Assembly; Nehemiah, Yale class of 1732, had chosen to become a minister; and David during the winter of 1737–1738 decided that he too should study for the ministry at Yale.

The diary fails to reveal, however, the full reasons for his choice. Did he want mainly to escape from the farm that his father had assumed he would work?
