Did he choose the ministry for the social rank that it assured? Or did he want simply the liberal education that went with preparing for the clerical life? Ten years later he wondered about the sincerity of his choice: "I became very strict and watchful over my thoughts, words, and actions; and thought I must be sober indeed, because I designed to devote myself to the ministry; and imagined I did dedicate myself to the Lord."[^003-note105] But whatever the cause of his doubts, it is more than likely that his choice of career had been greatly influenced not only by Nehemiah, who trained him for college, but also—at an earlier time in life—by his mother. As the three younger brothers, David, John, and Israel, all successively entered Yale with the ministry in mind, each must have felt somewhat pressed by the clerical tradition on their mother's side.

Nehemiah, however, had not at first been David's teacher. When David returned from his farm to Haddam in April of 1738, he had intended to prepare for college with Phineas Fiske (1682–1738), the family pastor. But Fiske died six months later, leaving David to study under Nehemiah. (Fiske's daughter Elizabeth was

<!-- p. 37 -->

Nehemiah's wife.) Most important of all, it was during this time that David found spiritual relief the likes of which he had never known before. After years of struggle and prolonged anxiety of soul he at last felt himself converted. According to the diary for July 12, 1739, he had that day withdrawn from the open into a "dark thick grove" for prayer, and there a sense of "unspeakable glory" filled his soul. As a result, he felt that he had entered a "new world" in which everything appeared with "a different aspect from what it was wont to do."[^003-note106] He was prepared to leave his family with high hopes for the coming year at Yale.

#### Evangelists

Still, it was a sad young man who in September of 1739 found himself at Yale. Brainerd, who was twenty-one at the time, was obliged to live amongst other freshmen, most of whom were seventeen and younger. Moreover, he had by custom to endure hazing from upperclassmen, although few were older than he. The drunken and frivolous behavior of his classmates greatly distressed him, and when an epidemic of measles struck the college his misery was compounded: he had briefly to go back to Haddam to get well. The effects of this illness, together with the rigors of his studies, so weakened him that by spring he was exhausted. In August he was told to go home once again, for by now it was clear that he suffered from a grim disease: he had begun to spit blood.

Brainerd went back to Haddam for two months, and on returning to New Haven in November, 1740, found the atmosphere changed. The English evangelist George Whitefield (1714–1770) had preached to the students at the college so effectively that many now were deeply concerned for their souls. In addition, Whitefield had opposed the rigid forms into which religion had fallen, had spoken against the spiritual paralysis that had gradually overcome New England, and had criticized both Yale and Harvard for their lack of piety and zeal. "As for the Universities," Whitefield later wrote, "I believe, it may be said, that their light is become darkness. Darkness that may be felt, and is complained of by the most godly misters."[^003-note107] Edwards, who was

<!-- p. 38 -->

not a close friend of Whitefield, but who had allowed him to preach at Northampton just a few days before the visit to New Haven, agreed with this criticism of Yale: and Brainerd, as the diary shows, soon found himself torn between such views and those of the college administration.

When Thomas Clap (1703–1767), Rector of Yale College, made it clear that he opposed the Awakening, a group of students began imitating Whitefield's enthusiasm and evangelical zeal. In spite of college and civil authorities, they formed their own congregation, left the established church, and preached in dissenting pulpits: and though Edwards, by his own stance, had encouraged these enthusiasts, he felt that they had gone too far. Indeed, what interests Edwards about Brainerd's life at Yale is that the young man, who was clearly a leader of this group, later confessed that he had been wrong to do these things and had given up enthusiasm for the warm, steady principles of religion that Edwards himself preached.

Brainerd's passions had been stirred, however, by men who were older than he, and among these were Gilbert Tennent (1703–1764), Ebenezer Pemberton (1705–1777), and James Davenport (1716–1757), all of whom disrupted student life at Yale. Tennent, who in March, 1741, had arrived in New Haven to carry on Whitefield's work, was then thirty-eight years old. Born in County Armagh, Ireland, he was a graduate of the Presbyterian "Log College" at Neshaminy, Pennsylvania, which his father, William Tennent, had founded in 1728. Greatly impressed by the evangelical zeal that the Dutch Reformed pastor Theodore Frelinghuysen had brought to the parishes near New Brunswick, he had also been strongly influenced by Whitefield, who backed his New England tour. But it was Tennent's wild appearance—his voice and manner of preaching—that made a marked impression on all his hearers. Of a sermon this Irish evangelist delivered in New York, November 14, 1739, Whitefield wrote in his journal: "He went to the bottom indeed, and did not daub with untempered Mortar … Hypocrites must either soon be converted or enraged at his preaching. He is a son of thunder, and I find doth not fear the faces of men."[^003-note108] The effect of his preaching, what is more, was even greater than that of Whitefield. Certain

<!-- p. 39 -->

Boston ministers declared that in three months' time more than one thousand persons concerned for their souls visited Tennent, who before he left New England had preached in twenty other Massachusetts and Connecticut towns—always with great effect. Within a single week at New Haven he had given more than seventeen sermons from the pulpit of the First Church, then held by Joseph Noyes (1688–1761). Tennent frequently preached in the college hall as well.

We are told by Samuel Hopkins (1721–1803), then a senior, that a band of students had followed Tennent on foot when he went to preach at Milford: and though Brainerd, then a sophomore, may or may not have been among them, he soon became known for visiting fellow students for prayer. Two other undergraduates, Samuel Buell (1716–1798) and David Youngs (1719–1751?), worked with Brainerd in his self-appointed task, the three forming a mission of their own. Hopkins, who at the start resented their calls, finally went one day to an adjoining room, took up Isaac Watt's version of the Psalms, and in tears read aloud the fifty-first, marking Brainerd's first conversion. But it was Tennent to whom credit for Hopkins' conversion was ultimately owed. Although Hopkins later forsook Tennent "to go and live with Mr. Edwards," it was Tennent who had paved the way.[^003-note109] Moreover, it was Tennent's zeal that had paved the way for Ebenezer Pemberton at Yale.

Pemberton, who was a graduate of Harvard College in 1721, may once have seemed safe enough to be allowed to speak at the college in New Haven; but by 1741 he was known to preach with such conviction and force that crowds followed him in the roads. As pastor of the Presbyterian church in New York, he set an example that reflects the growing momentum of the Awakening. When in 1739 Whitefield had come to New York, Pemberton was the only clergyman to welcome him into his pulpit. Later, at the high point of the New Haven tour in 1741, Pemberton preached in the college hall a sermon that vividly portrayed how far his judgment had been swayed. With little thought for the consequences, he exhorted students to embrace Christ without regard for the things of this earth. Knowledge other than that which could be derived from conviction of conscience, he declared, need not

<!-- p. 40 -->

be taken seriously. Indeed, the study of divinity itself could act as a hindrance to grace. Taking his text from 1 Corinthians 2:2 ("For I determined not to know anything among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified") he gave an interpretation that was literal from the start. Moreover, how far students were willing to go in their approval of Pemberton's views was soon made clear; for only three undergraduates did not contribute to the cost of printing the text. Brainerd ordered six copies, as did Buell and Youngs, and Hopkins ordered eight.[^003-note110] Pemberton's influence, in short, was profound.

There is no indication in the diary, however, that Brainerd at the time of Pemberton's visit thought of becoming a missionary. In spite of illness and bouts of melancholia, he had by then reached the top of his college class and clearly did not intend to take up a lowly career. But later Pemberton did pave the way for Brainerd to take up the missionary life. It was Pemberton who asked the Society in Scotland to hire Brainerd when as punishment for revival activities he was expelled from Yale. It was Pemberton who preached his ordination sermon (June 12, 1744), and who arranged for parts of the manuscript diary to be published in 1746. Pemberton, one might say, did as much as he possibly could (perhaps by way of compensation) to restore Brainerd's self-confidence and to start him off on a new life.[^003-note111] But Pemberton was not the most extreme evangelist who in 1741 had shattered the New Haven air. By far the most dangerous was James Davenport, a man who strongly influenced Brainerd and whom many considered not to be entirely sane.

As a member of the Yale class of 1732, Davenport had taken his degree at the age of sixteen and was one of the youngest men ever to be graduated from the college. He was the great grandson of John Davenport, founder of New Haven Colony, and in 1741 was minister at Southold, Long Island. That summer the thirty-three-year-old bachelor had crossed over the waters of the sound to preach in Connecticut, even though the previous May the New Haven County Association of Ministers had passed a resolution against itinerants. No pastor, it was held, could preach

<!-- p. 41 -->

in any parish "not his own charge" without permission of the settled minister.[^003-note112] That resolution, of course, merely expressed the wishes of the Association. Connecticut still lacked a law that could keep Davenport out: and the result was disastrous. When he came to New Haven in September, just before commencement, he denounced Joseph Noyes from his own pulpit and advised the congregation to leave him for good.[^003-note113]

It has been said of Davenport that this deranged man "produced a powerful effect upon the mind of David Brainerd … though an effect which was at best of a mixed character."[^003-note114] Ezra Stiles (then a boy soon to attend Yale) had heard the Long Island evangelist and was taken aback by the "indecent, mad, and blasphemous religion" that Davenport preached.[^003-note115] Nevertheless, it was not long before the boys in the college increasingly came to resent the sermons they were forced to hear from Noyes in the New Haven church. When one student was called to account for missing Sunday service, he said that he had stayed away "because of the coldness of the air and of the preacher,"[^003-note116] and the New Light students, who thoroughly disliked Noyes, were happy to have this sentiment so vividly expressed. But the Yale trustees saw that other cases of disrespect were likely to follow, and as a result, adopted regulations for the punishment of students who asserted that tutors, trustees, or Rector Thomas Clap were "unconverted, unexperienced and unskillful guides in matters of religion." During commencement week, 1741, while Davenport raged and fumed, matters came to a head, and on September 9, commencement day, it was voted "that if any student of this College shall directly or indirectly say, that the Rector, either of the Trustees or Tutors are hypocrites, carnal or unconverted men, he shall for the first offence make a public confession in the hall, and for the second offence be expelled."[^003-note117]

<!-- p. 42 -->

In the wake of Davenport's excesses, with the college broken and divided, this rule, it was thought, made sense. It was also thought that Edwards, the commencement speaker of the day, would come down hard on a movement that had gone too far. Such, however, proved not to be the case. Edwards came forth not to criticize the evangelists, as the trustees had expected, but to defend their work. With Brainerd in the assembled crowd, listening to every word, the man who had described with care the stirrings in his own Northampton church in 1735 now rose to insist that the current excesses in themselves are "no argument that the work in general is not the work of the Spirit of God." The horrors of the revival, Edwards declared, are no sign that the Holy Spirit is not at work. Moreover, such excesses as visions, tears, and the condemning of others as unconverted are not incompatible with an authentic work of the Spirit. "And here in particular," said Edwards, "it is no evidence that a work is not the work of God, if many that are subjects of it … are guilty of too great a forwardness to censure others as unconverted."[^003-note118]

Although the excesses of the New Lights were in Edwards' speech condemned (with a warning against spiritual pride), the evangelists received in this commencement address the strongest possible support. Indeed, with Yale reeling under Davenport's lash, with Noyes and others subjected to bitter attack, Edwards seemed now to be hallooing the hounds: and to this extent he set the stage for what was to come. He must share the blame (along with Tennent, Pemberton, and Davenport) for the events that led to Brainerd's expulsion from Yale.

#### Adversaries

In the following winter (1741–1742) Brainerd broke the rule enacted at commencement and was heard to say that Chauncey Whittelsey (1717–1787), tutor in the college, had "no more grace than a chair." He was also reported to have said that he wondered that Rector Clap "did not drop down dead" for fining the students who had followed Gilbert Tennent to Milford. The second charge Brainerd denied, but because he would not confess the first offence in Hall he was expelled. Edwards, who took a

<!-- p. 43 -->

distinctly detached view of the affair, thought that it was "injuriously required of him … to make a public confession … for what he said only in private conversation." However, Edwards then judiciously took the blame off others (himself included) with the remark that "Brainerd had the unhappiness to have a tincture of that intemperate indiscreet zeal … to the habitual temper of his mind."[^003-note119] At no point would Edwards blame the evangelists for his young friend's plight. And though Brainerd wrote the trustees a letter of apology for what he had said, he was not allowed to take the degree with his class. Moreover, the degree was never awarded, although Brainerd Hall now stands in New Haven on Prospect Hill.

What is remarkable about the affair, and the punishment meted out, is that Brainerd (although he confessed when accused) was brought down on indirect evidence, or hearsay. Indeed, it was only by the slightest chance and by a series of unfortunate circumstances that the affair took place at all, for Brainerd had not made his remark as part of a public campaign to stir up excess zeal. Quite to the contrary. On the occasion itself, after Tutor Whittelsey had led the college in prayer and had retired from the chapel (leaving Brainerd with one or two friends in the hall), a freshman overheard Brainerd make the remark, "He has no more grace than a chair." But the freshman could not tell of whom the remark was made. This meddling undergraduate then told a woman, through whose gossip the authorities were alerted, and these authorities, by intimidating Brainerd's friends, drew from them a confession that it was Whittelsey whom Brainerd had so severely judged. Not content with Brainerd's forthright admission of guilt, however, the college administrators then insisted that the self-confessed student should shame himself by a public confession before the whole body of students, and it was at this juncture that Brainerd drew the line: he refused to comply. Later on, when by full confession of the wrong to the authorities, and by the powerful intercession of Edwards and others he again asked to be forgiven, the request was denied, and subsequent efforts to regain admission show how deeply injured he continued to feel for the rest of his life.

In the opinion of Thomas Brainerd, David's collateral descendant,

<!-- p. 44 -->

the repentant student "ought to have been forgiven at once." Looking back at the event from the mid-nineteenth century and declaring himself at the time to be a strong advocate of "order and subordination among college students," he went on to say that "the authorities of Yale College allowed no candid discernment to discriminate between a courser and a plough-horse,—between a sensitive and high-spirited genius and plodding obstinacy,—and, by their persistence, obliterated the name of David Brainerd forever from their 'Triennial Catalogues.'" Whether Brainerd or the college lost most by this omission, he continued, "I think the world has long since decided."[^003-note120]

There can be no doubt, wrote Thomas Brainerd, that the missionary's life was "shortened by his college persecution." A section of the diary reveals, we are told, "the most intense and overwhelming mental suffering from the stigma fastened on him":[^003-note121] and that section, which was part of the manuscript diary that Thomas Brainerd then possessed, but which Edwards for reasons of his own had excluded from the printed text, is quoted for July 9, 1743, at New Haven:

> I was still occupied with some business depending on certain grandees for performance. Alas! how much men may lord and tyrannize over their fellow countrymen, yet pretend that all their treatment of them is full of lenity and kindness,—that they owe them some special regard,—that they would hardly treat another with so much tenderness, and the like. Like the Holy Court of Inquisition, when they put a poor innocent to the rack, they tell him that what they do is all for the benefit of his soul! Lord, deliver my soul from this temper![^003-note122]

There were several separate diaries from which Edwards gleaned his material for the 1749 printed text. Two of these manuscript volumes, which together made up one hundred and twenty pages, were in Thomas Brainerd's hands as late as 1865. One was a record of David's religious experiences, which Edwards had copied in large part, and the other included the history of the struggle with Yale. Of this second journal, we are informed,

<!-- p. 45 -->

Edwards published "not more than a fourth part."[^003-note123] It had been written at Kaunaumeek from May to November, 1743, and its record of the trip to New Haven between July 2 and July 25 was entirely left out. Therefore, the fragment that Thomas Brainerd has preserved in his *Life of John Brainerd* is greatly to be valued, for it reveals a sense of outrage and frustration that is not to be found in Edwards' text. Moreover, this fragment from what can only be called the "lost journal" of David Brainerd suggests that a bitter face-to-face confrontation took place between Brainerd and the authorities—making Edwards' job all the more difficult; for under such conditions none could convince Yale to grant Brainerd his degree. We shall never know, however, more than the fragment reveals, for Thomas Brainerd, although he intended to publish the whole manuscript, never did so. "It is justly severe on the college authorities," he wrote of the since-vanished document; "they broke his heart."[^003-note124]

It should be stressed, nevertheless, that in spite of the grief and outrage that the fragment from the lost journal reveals, Chauncey Whittelsey was innocent of Brainerd's accusation, and Brainerd must have been thoroughly ashamed when he realized that this was true. Whittelsey, who tutored in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, had started his teaching in the college when Brainerd first arrived. Only six months older than his accuser, he was relatively moderate in his opposition to the revival. Moreover, he was much like Brainerd in that he kept a diary in which, at the time he was licensed to preach (September 30, 1740), he expressed the ardent wish that he be made fit for service in the church.[^003-note125] But the excesses of revivalism offended his sense of decorum—his conviction that reason is superior to experience. He belonged, moreover, to a family that condemned the Awakening in Connecticut, a fact which may account for his moderate tone in prayer.

Whittelsey's father, Samuel, was a friend and cousin-in-law of Charles Chauncy (1705–1787), Boston's greatest opponent of the Awakening: and for these men, as for others of Arminian tendency, religion had always to be tested by reasonable persuasion. "The general rule of the divine conduct as the moral governor

<!-- p. 46 -->

of the world," Chauncey Whittelsey later wrote, "is to grant more grace, more power and richer advantages to those who have been faithful to their past improvements."[^003-note126] For Brainerd, needless to say, such a theory had little to do with his own experience of grace—with the sheer miracle of divine intervention; but in rashly declaring that Whittelsey lacked grace, Brainerd had stepped beyond the judgment of charity. What is more, his remarks had been carelessly made about one of the most learned and effective teachers at Yale.

Whittelsey, it should be said, was greatly admired in the college, both by New and Old Lights alike. Although his prayers may not have been flavored with evangelical zeal his range of learning was wide. Indeed, his knowledge of the liberal arts was rivaled only by his knowledge of the sciences, and his ability to impart both humanistic and scientific truths could be equaled by no other teacher in New Haven. Ezra Stiles, who as an undergraduate had attended Whittelsey's classes, later said of this unusual man that he had amassed through laborious reading "a great treasure of wisdom," that his "very happy talent at instruction" allowed him to teach with success "in every branch of knowledge," and that all agreed he should be counted in the end "among the most learned and eminent tutors of Yale College."[^003-note127]

Whittelsey remained a tutor, however, for only six years (1739–1745), after which he took up a business. By 1747, the year that Brainerd died, this teacher turned importer had been asked to manage a lottery by which sums could be raised for new college buildings. What is more, between 1751 and 1756 he was Deputy from New Haven to the Connecticut General Assembly, and in 1758 the First Church on the Green recorded a unanimous vote to ask him to become co-pastor with the aging Reverend Noyes. Accordingly, on March 1, Whittelsey left the secular world and was ordained minister (six months past his fortieth birthday). After the death of Noyes, three years later, Whittelsey continued as sole pastor until July 24, 1787, when he died in his seventieth year.

How, then, may we compare the accuser and the accused? Unlike

<!-- p. 47 -->

Brainerd, Whittelsey lived a long and prosperous life. It was a life, moreover, in which piety and prosperity seemed always to go hand in hand. Although his first wife died when she was thirty-five, and five of his fourteen children perished in infancy, he managed to persevere with courage, stamina, and charm. Stiles, in a funeral sermon that might readily be compared with Edwards' oration on Brainerd, commended Whittelsey's "order, zeal, and assiduity in the duties of the pastoral office," his "singular talent at accommodating himself with ease to all characters, high and low, rich and poor," and "his … charity to his fellow Christians."[^003-note128] It was also said of Whittelsey that he was a man of great dignity who joined integrity and philanthropy to an accurate knowledge of men and affairs.[^003-note129] In short, he stood for all that Thomas Clap had intended his graduates to be.

As opposed to Brainerd, whose health and temper had never been even, and who spent what money he had on education and books for others, Whittelsey enjoyed robust health, an even-tempered mind, and left an estate valued at £3500 (which included a library of more than two hundred volumes). Indeed, his ministry was later described as "prosperous for the age in which he labored."[^003-note130] At the First Church on the Green (under Whittelsey's pastoral care) one was able to forget that surge of revivalism which had been ushered in by Whitefield, reenforced by Tennent, and compounded by Pemberton and Davenport in their misguided efforts to deal with students at Yale. One was even able to forget that Thomas Clap, once a strong opponent of revivalism, had later changed sides.

In the Whittelsey affair, Clap had wanted to protect Yale; he had felt at first that the evangelists were his enemies. He had further assumed that students who shared their views were also enemies, with the result that his high-handed methods brought trouble not only to Brainerd but to others as well. At the time of Brainerd's expulsion Clap was thirty-eight years old. By 1750, curiously enough, he had changed his stand and had joined those who supported the revivals. However, nothing that he said or did

<!-- p. 48 -->

in the 1740s intimated that he would one day invite Whitefield to New Haven, a gesture that would mark the end of a stormy career.

That career had begun on February 22, 1726, when in Windham. Connecticut, Clap was installed at the Congregational Church. There he became known as a strict taskmaster of indomitable will: and though the members of his Hock endured him for fourteen years, when he accepted the Yale rector ship in 1739 it was said that "they acted like boys let out of school."[^003-note131] When Clap was installed as the new Rector on April 2, 1740, the "Collegiate School" (as the college was then called) needed desperately to be given new life, and to this task he gave all his energy and strength. With a teaching staff that included only three or four tutors, he embarked on an ambitious program for Yale. Soon after taking office he proposed a more liberal charter, granted by the Assembly in 1745. In addition, he drew up a new code of laws and made plans to construct buildings of which the college had been in great need for a long time. But he held, at the same time, that "the principal design and institution of this college was to educate persons for the work of the ministry,"[^003-note132] and to this end had cast off the liberalism of Harvard, where in 1722 he had taken his degree. On the whole, his administration was two-sided and a mixed blessing for Yale. Indeed, his tenure has been described as "one of the most decisively constructive, as well as one of the most troubled, in Yale history."[^003-note133] Students who did not follow the rules were made to feel his wrath: and Brainerd, it should be stressed, was just one of many who were either fined, expelled, or threatened with the loss of their degrees.

On the student who failed to attend chapel "because of the coldness of the air and of the preacher," Clap had imposed a fine of five shillings. Two years later, in 1744, John and Ebenezer Cleveland were expelled from college for going to a Separate meeting (while at home on vacation) in Canterbury. But on every occasion the Rector did not win the day. Once when some seniors had taken up a subscription for reprinting Locke's *Essay on Toleration*, Clap demanded a public confession of their sins or the loss of their degrees; but when a student who refused to confess

<!-- p. 49 -->

found his name missing from the catalogue at commencement, he was able to win his degree by threatening to appeal to the King in Council. At another time, when some students asked that one of their number not be punished so severely as to ruin his health, Clap fined the petitioners severely; in response they turned over his horseblock and privy—forcing him to take a "ride to Hartford for about a fortnight to give them time to cool."[^003-note134] Brainerd, compared with some others, gave in with relative calm to Clap's rule.

Still, this formidable man remained "the venerable Rector," even to those who endured his fines or struggled against his policies. "The only serious defect in his presidential character," wrote Timothy Dwight, "was that he was prone to consider men as boys."[^003-note135] There were, however, other defects as well—not least of which was an utter lack of charm. "Had he been possessed of politeness," Ezra Stiles explained, "he would have figured as one of the lights, one of the first literary characters of his age." But Clap was "determined, resolute, firm, immoveable—even to absolute despotism,"[^003-note136] and these characteristics did not endear him to all. When he died, leaving Yale in a shaky state, those who had known him felt obliged to render a verdict, and Stiles (who had distrusted Clap's conversion to New Lightism) wrote Chauncey Whittelsey the following report:

> For a while his hobby horse ran away with him and who is there that is not hobby horsical at times. But he was truly a man of literature and great abilities, and his Presidency from 1740 to 1752 did him honor; in 1757 he was a little befogged in the atmosphere of New Lightism and yet was never a New Light. This was his natural despotism, and high notions of dominion wro't him much mischief and did him not the benefit he expected. Though no great classical scholar, and a man of no politeness, yet he had many excellent endowments … You and I knew him perfectly—he was once a good friend to us. From 1742 to 1752 I found him my best friend; and though upon his political conversion his love waxed cool, yet I still honor the memory of my once Micaenas…. But what shall

<!-- p. 50 -->

  we say of that transmutation he underwent from 1754 to 1757?[^003-note137]

Clap is finally described by Stiles as a man whose "reasoning powers were good and well improved." "As to his person," Stiles continued, "he was not tall, yet being thickset he appeared rather large and bulky…. He was a calm, still, judicious great man."[^003-note138] He was also, however, a great adversary—a man who without remorse disrupted human lives, and in Brainerd's case he disrupted a life that had never been filled with joy.

Brainerd, of course, had faults of his own which may have hardened Clap against him, for the undergraduate had never embraced Yale. His freshman year, even before the measles epidemic had struck, he confessed that he "longed for death" in spite of his admittance to the college. The scorn that he showed for his classmates, on the one hand, and for his tutor, on the other, showed traits of character not to be entirely condoned. But one suspects that events of his early life had shaped his view of the world long before he got to Yale. He may have felt abandoned—even rejected—and as a result disliked himself and was intolerant of others. One suspects, above all, that his disease of the lungs was well under way long before he first spat blood; that his health was bad when his college days began. This would help to explain those character faults that did not endear him to others, and would also make it easier to understand why he reacted as he did to the emotional upheaval that cut across his first college year.

What cannot be known, however, is the full extent of Brainerd's activities at Yale. Because he destroyed his college diaries before he died, and because Thomas Brainerd lost the journal in which Clap and the others were condemned, little is known about how far Brainerd pushed his enthusiasm at the time. In his published diary he admits to having attended a Separate meeting and records for posterity that after he left college he was "more refined from some imprudencies and indecent heats."[^003-note139] Beyond that, however, not a fragment of evidence remains on which to build a case. Edwards, as Thomas Brainerd has shown, had access to the since-lost journal, but did not print extracts from it. Moreover,

<!-- p. 51 -->

if the charges against Brainerd were exaggerated, Edwards did not say so: rather, he defended his friend on the grounds of "youth," stating that the wayward undergraduate (who was considerably older than his classmates) was "not only young in years, but very young in religion and experience."[^003-note140] Above all, Edwards stressed the extent to which Brainerd abhorred himself for the part he played in the affair: the repentant side of his nature is stressed throughout; for Edwards wanted to tone down the controversy with Yale.

It is not possible fully to explain Brainerd's college behavior; nor is it possible to suggest much more than the diary reveals. But what has been preserved from the diary is considerable, and what the text shows is that in spite of his spiritual views—in spite of his conversion—he could not maintain at college a vision of the world that allowed him to see everything as "new" and "different" from what he had known before. The world of his youth, of his pre-conversion years, seemed always to haunt him. Moreover, the period before he actually took up missionary work was perhaps the darkest in his life. Smarting from the pain of expulsion, with no real activity to keep his mind off it, he wrote: "I thought … I had no power to stand for the cause of God, but was almost 'afraid of the shaking of a leaf.'"[^003-note141]

#### Friends

Among the friends to whom Brainerd immediately turned was Jedediah Mills (1697–1776), pastor at Ripton—ten miles west of New Haven. In April of 1742, soon after his dismissal from Yale, Brainerd went to live and study with Mills, who for eighteen years had eked out a slender living by preparing young men for college. Ordained in 1724, two years after finishing at Yale, Mills had gained a wide reputation as a teacher; but in 1742 opinion ran against him, and he lost influence with Yale—mainly because of his strong reputation for evangelical zeal.[^003-note142] Brainerd, nevertheless, with Mills' support, asked a council of ministers at Hartford to intercede for him with Rector Clap and the trustees—although he must have known ahead of time that the council would fail. The events of the time were working against him. Because

<!-- p. 52 -->

of the increase of lay preachers, a law now provided that "no person who has not been educated at Yale College, or at Harvard College in Cambridge, or some Foreign College or University, shall be allowed the special privileges of the established ministers of the government,"[^003-note143] and this law must have increased Brainerd's efforts to gain his degree. Another law, passed by the Hartford Assembly in the spring of 1742, outlawed itinerant preaching. No minister could preach in the parish of another without permission, and no consociation of ministers could license candidates for the ministry to preach within the jurisdiction of another. The Assembly, which opposed the revival as a threat to law and order, realized that only through such a law could they restrict the influence of those consociations of ministers that favored revival preachers and sent them as itinerants throughout the country. Therefore, Brainerd, who was first an itinerant preacher before he became a missionary, had either to break the law or remain silent.

That decision he soon made, as he turned to a friend who without hesitation encouraged him to break the law. Joseph Bellamy (1719–1790), minister at Bethlehem, was a year younger than Brainerd. Although a moderate New Light, he encouraged itinerant preaching in spite of the law against it. He not only invited itinerants to preach at Bethlehem, but also influenced Brainerd's decision to preach in the districts that were hostile to New Light ministers. He was a close friend of Edwards and became one of Brainerd's closest friends. (According to one of Edwards' letters to John Erskine, Bellamy is the "particularly dear … friend" to whom Brainerd refers throughout the diary.)[^003-note144]

As a member of the Yale class of 1735, Bellamy had been graduated at the age of sixteen. He had then studied with Edwards for two years and was only eighteen when he accepted the call from Bethlehem in 1740. Throughout the summer of 1742 he and Brainerd shared living quarters and preached in the barn that they used as a meetinghouse. That July Brainerd and Reuben Judd, a college friend, were licensed to preach by the Association of the Eastern District of Fairfield County, a group of New Lights who opposed the established New Haven Consociation and

<!-- p. 53 -->

who wanted a licensing body of their own. Because Brainerd had been licensed as a probationer, he was not yet allowed to administer baptism or communion, but he could preach as an authorized minister within the Association's district. If he left the district he would have to hide from authorities, and with Bellamy's help he often did.

It is curious, however, that Brainerd should have taken up with Bellamy, who even more than Mills could only harm his cause with Yale. In 1740 Bellamy had angered Thomas Clap by entering at once into the spirit of the revival. Later, when he took up itinerant preaching not only in Connecticut but also in neighboring colonies, he had inspired further wrath. But all who knew him were by no means appalled. Benjamin Trumbull, who followed Bellamy at Yale by fourteen years, has described the Bethlehem minister as "a large well built man of a commanding appearance who had a smooth, strong voice, and could fill the largest house without any unnatural elevation." It was Trumbull's opinion, what is more, that Bellamy had "a truly great mind."[^003-note145] Others who knew him, however, held a more negative point of view. Payson Williston (Yale class of 1783) wrote in 1855 from personal recollections that Bellamy was prone to "great natural severity of temper." "He was a capital teacher," said Williston, "and yet I have heard of instances in which young men who went to study with him were so unpleasantly impressed by his abrupt and dogmatical manner, that they refused to remain with him a single day."[^003-note146] Of those who condemned Bellamy outright, Ezra Stiles was the most severe. Stiles lists more than a dozen ministers whom Bellamy had "gutted," "stabbed," or persecuted in one way or another because they were obnoxious to him. "He was of a haughty, domineering temper," wrote Stiles, "and till of late years unmercifully censorious of his brethren in the ministry and others who opposed him."[^003-note147]

Bellamy remained throughout his life a controversial figure, having taken to an extreme that tendency to censure others which had brought Brainerd down at Yale. Like Brainerd, moreover, he had turned to Edwards for consolation and advice: "He was highly carried away with New Lightism in 1741," Stiles observes,

<!-- p. 54 -->

"but soon recovered himself from the extravagancies of those times by the friendly counsels of President Edwards, to whom he was greatly attached."[^003-note148] But Brainerd was not like Bellamy. Nor was he the sort of person who should become an itinerant preacher, much less go into the wilderness by himself. As the diary clearly reveals, Brainerd's itinerant preaching, followed by his life as a missionary, must be seen not as a positive step in his career but as a result of the disruption of his career; for he continued to hope that Yale would allow him to finish his course of studies and take his degree. He could not give up the hope of gaining the full credentials needed for a settled ministry. Far more than he was willing to admit, he needed the stability of a settled life and the closeness of friends.

Of those to whom he turned for friendship the most reliable was Jonathan Dickinson (1688–1747), a man who differed from Bellamy on every count. Dickinson, then the leading Presbyterian in New Jersey, had paid a visit to New Haven in February, 1742, and had taken up Brainerd's cause. He may also have discussed with Brainerd the possibility of a missionary career, for Dickinson was by then one of the commissioners for the Society in Scotland, which was now looking for a volunteer. Whether or not Brainerd actually told Dickinson at this time that he would accept such a post cannot be known, but his activities for the following year indicate that he had. From May of 1742 until March of 1743 he traveled more than twelve hundred miles on horseback—preparing himself for the missionary work yet to come: and when he traveled in New Jersey he stayed at Dickinson's house.

Dickinson played a part in Brainerd's life that was equal to, if not greater than, the role of Edwards himself. Had Brainerd toward the end not sought out Jerusha Edwards in Northampton, he might well have remained at Elizabethtown and died in Dickinson's house. No other man, apart from Edwards, took such an interest in Brainerd's plight. None was so vividly aware of how perfectly he served the New Side Presbyterian cause. He personified, on the one hand, what the Tennents' Log College (which Dickinson now disliked) had failed to produce, and, on the other hand, what Dickinson's own college, Yale, had refused to tolerate. In short, he stood for what a new college in the middle colonies

<!-- p. 55 -->

might strive to produce, a sound reason for founding the College of New Jersey (which became the goal of Dickinson's life).

Toward such a goal, however, Dickinson had long been heading, before the need for a college had been stressed by Brainerd's plight. From 1709, when he was ordained pastor of the Elizabethtown church, he had felt uneasy with its strict Congregational organization. By 1717 he had been able to persuade the congregation to join the presbytery of Philadelphia, and as moderator of the Synod of 1721 he had insured that the liberal voice prevail. In addition, he at first gave the Tennents' Log College his full support: when the "Old Side" Presbyterians virtually blocked from ordination graduates of that college, he left the Philadelphia body and organized the Synod of New York. He also convinced many "New Side" brethren of the need for an institution that could train men for their ministry, and he was determined that the new college take a liberal Presbyterian stand.[^003-note149] Therefore, when the College of New Jersey was chartered in October of 1746, Dickinson was chosen president, and when the door was opened at the end of May, 1747, classes were held in his house. Because Brainerd was in residence that year, he is considered to be the first student enrolled.

According to David Dudley Field, Princeton College was founded because of Brainerd's expulsion from Yale. In 1857 Field gave the following firsthand account to support his claim: "I once heard the Hon. John Dickinson … son of the Rev. Mr. Dickinson, of Norwalk, say, that the establishment of Princeton College was owing to the sympathy felt for David Brainerd, because the authorities of Yale College would not give him his degree, and that the plan of the college was drawn up in his father's house."[^003-note150] Archibald Alexander also makes much of Brainerd, while at the same time giving Aaron Burr the position of co-founder. "Messrs. Dickinson and Burr," he maintains, "took the lead in this enterprise." He then goes on to say: "Both these distinguished divines were graduates of Yale College; but just at this time their minds probably experienced some alienation from their alma mater on account of the harsh treatment which Mr. David Brainerd had received from the officers of that college." Alexander,

<!-- p. 56 -->

in some closing remarks, concludes that "the attachment of all the members of the New York Synod to Mr. Brainerd was warm, and deservedly so," and that the expulsion had probably "quickened the zeal of these excellent men to get up a college of their own."[^003-note151]

Alexander, like Field, also offered a firsthand account: "Some years ago," he declared, he had heard "the relict [^003-note152] of the late Dr. Scott, of New Brunswick, say that when she was a little girl she heard the Rev. Mr. Burr declare in her father's house in Newark, 'if it had not been for the treatment received by Mr. Brainerd at Yale, New Jersey College would never have been erected.'"[^003-note153] It was, however, Thomas Brainerd who in summing up the evidence made the final claim: "This testimony of the Rev. Dr. Alexander so corroborates the statements of the Rev. Dr. Field," he wrote, "that we may regard the question as settled, that the expulsion of David Brainerd from Yale led to the founding of Princeton College."[^003-note154] The Brainerd tradition—well into the nineteenth century—remained strong.

Brainerd, of course, was not the sole reason that the college was founded, but there can be little doubt that Dickinson and Burr used his case to their advantage. (When Clap had complained that the New York Synod was receiving under its care members of Yale College who had left under censure, he clearly meant Brainerd.) Burr, like Dickinson, had also pled for Brainerd at Yale, having gone in 1743 to the commencement at which Brainerd's class was graduated, hoping to have him restored.[^003-note155]

Only two years older than Brainerd, Aaron Burr had taken his degree at nineteen, had been granted a graduate scholarship, and had gone on from Yale to a prosperous church. By 1742 he was widely known, having been installed in the Presbyterian Church of Newark in 1738. After Dickinson died in 1747 he was chosen president of the College of New Jersey, and with that institution under his command had, in 1752, married Edwards' third daughter, Esther, younger sister of Jerusha. Burr was thirty-six and Esther was twenty-one. Neither was immune to the numerous

<!-- p. 57 -->

diseases of the time. Esther, at twenty-six, died of a smallpox vaccination. Burr, only a year after he had moved the College from Newark to Princeton, died at forty-one "of a nervous fever," leaving two orphaned children behind.[^003-note156] One, his name-sake, later gained notorious fame.

Among those who had looked to Burr for advice was David's brother John Brainerd, a frequent visitor to the Burr house. Although Burr himself was not inclined toward missionary work, he had inspired both David and John to persevere in that task, and both had looked upon this man as a close friend. A question that must be asked, however, is whether or not Burr *should* have given these brothers the same advice. Although John faced mission work with some calm, David clearly did not. As the diary reveals, his ambitions as a scholar had now to give way to the role he took on as an obscure missionary, and in this role he loathed having to "give up all for gone."[^003-note157] But what biographers have not sufficiently stressed is that he need not have gone at all; for he had already shown—before his mission work began—that he was greatly in demand at home.

#### Associates

When in January of 1743 Brainerd stopped at Stonington, Connecticut, he faced his first major challenge after leaving Yale. Joseph Fish (1705–1781), Harvard class of 1728, had for a decade been secure in the North Stonington parish. Then in 1741 Davenport had invaded the town and had turned Fish's congregation against him. Although Fish had been active in the revivals, he was a preacher of scholarly bent. His sermons, it was said, "smelt of the lamp": and he came out of the clash with Davenport despairing of his own salvation. (In December of 1742 he had told his parishioners that he could no longer preach.)[^003-note158] But immediately Brainerd arrived and preached to the rebellious people, the matter was turned round. Fish soon resumed his pulpit and went on to serve for forty more years. Although faced with sporadic discord now and then, he remained until the end—running for a time an Indian school in the town—and he owed

<!-- p. 58 -->

his survival to Brainerd, whose triumph over Davenport's work had saved the day.

This incident at Stonington is given limited space in the diary, but it is important, for it shows how strong in his own world Brainerd could be. What is more, it shows a side of Brainerd that is greatly to be admired: his willingness to lend a hand to an associate in need of help. Coming so soon after the expulsion from Yale, the episode also shows that Brainerd could stand up when challenged—that he had in his own society the strength to endure.

When he went from Stonington to East Hampton, where in the winter of 1742–1743 he spent six weeks, he was again faced with the need to bring order out of strife, and again he showed that in spite of his commitment to the missionary life he was wanted, needed, and effective on his native ground. Recently disgraced in New Haven, Brainerd was now embraced by East Hampton, at the time a whaling village and one of the largest parishes on Long Island. This town too had been disrupted by Davenport; it needed a new preacher as well as calm advice. Moreover, the church, although originally established along Congregational lines in fellowship with the churches of Connecticut, was moving toward the Presbyterian pattern established in New York; so that Brainerd, as a Congregationalist with Presbyterian leanings, was regarded as the right man to manage the shift. During the time that he spent there, however, he did not encourage the town to offer him a livelihood; by then he was committed to the commissioners and to his coming work in the mission field. But this commitment, it should be said, had by now become a serious worry in his life.

Brainerd, of course, had been exposed to Indian ways as a boy. He had observed at a distance lowly native life along Connecticut's shores. But now at East Hampton he made a visit to Montauk Point, sixteen miles away on the east side of the island, where Azariah Horton presided over two towns containing one hundred and sixty-two souls, and it was here that he had to confront fully the "flatness" and "deadness" of his own response to Indian life.

When he first set out to see Horton's flock, he felt "some inward sweetness" on the road. That feeling, however, soon gave way to dread, and before he had left these people he was so undone by the "blackness" of his nature that he thought himself unfit

<!-- p. 59 -->

for the task ahead.[^003-note159] Never before had he seen at close hand such squalid conditions; never before had he fully understood what life amongst such people might be like. He had, moreover, in Horton an associate whom he observed in dire apprehension for his own success.

Azariah Horton (1715–1777) had like Brainerd been ordained by the New York Presbytery and was supported by the Society in Scotland. Of the class of 1735 at Yale, he had since 1741 been laboring among a struggling group of Long Island Indians who barely survived along the southern shore. But the enterprise was too vast and could not be managed. In addition to the two towns, Horton was responsible for scattered groups of Nantics, Mahicans, Pequots, and Naragansetts who lived along one hundred miles of sandy coast, and with these his ministry was especially weak. Indeed, of the four hundred souls under his complete domain, he baptized only forty-four children and thirty-five adults, and of these only twenty could be said to have given sound evidence of saving faith. Many fell prey to whiskey and rum, so that Horton, with little to show for his efforts, eventually had to give up.[^003-note160]

Brainerd sensed that Horton's efforts were futile. Although the diary does not say so, the decision in March of 1743 to leave East Hampton (where he had been "frequently invited" by whites to settle) must have been the most difficult in his life.[^003-note161] Certainly it sealed his commitment to the commissioners; it also cut him off from a lucrative post. In the years that followed he would yearn for a settled community; but by frequent contact with friends and associates, he was able to endure.

Among those who now entered his life was John Sergeant (1710–1749), missionary to the Housatonic Indians at Stock-bridge. Sergeant looms large in the diary not only because he trained Brainerd for his task but also because the Stockbridge mission set a standard for all others. Sergeant's Housatonics, unlike Horton's scattered tribes, were all housed in one town. Because Sergeant had only one tongue to master, he was able to control his people as Horton could not.

After taking his Yale degree in 1729, Sergeant was from 1731

<!-- p. 60 -->

to 1735 tutor at the college, where he also studied theology. But he was not bound for a settled church. In answer to an appeal from Samuel Hopkins and Stephen Williams, ministers at Springfield, and from Colonel John Stoddard of Northampton, the commissioners of Indian affairs had asked Sergeant to set up a mission post in the western colonial parts. These commissioners, who were also agents for the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in New England, had heard it said of Sergeant that "he had rather be employed as a missionary to the natives, if a door should open for it, than accept a call any English parish might give him": and so in September, 1734, he was offered the mission. Later he wrote that he had taken the job, among other reasons, because the "pains taken by those of the Romish Church, not only in other parts but also in America … should methinks excite us to emulation, who at least think we profess Christianity in much greater purity."[^003-note162]

These commissioners had also determined that the Upper Valley of the Housatonic River was ripe for mission work—mainly because of the concentration there of Mahicans, who had moved eastward when the Dutch had inhabited the west bank of the Hudson. These natives, of Algonquian heritage, called themselves Mahiccondas, or river people, and later were called Housatonics by the English, who found them to be friendly, few in number, and easy to manage. Because their chief, Konapot, was receptive to Christian doctrine, Sergeant with relative ease could set up a mission.

He had first gone to the natives at Great Barrington, using one Ebenezer Paupaumunk as an interpreter. Between October and November, 1734, he had then got the Stockbridge Indians to erect a building, which soon served as both a church and a school. By the time of his ordination he was well prepared to manage the mission for which the Society in Scotland also provided support.[^003-note163]

On August 31, 1735, when he was twenty-five, Sergeant was ordained at Deerfield in the presence of the governor of the colony and a large group of Indians and ministers. Not since the time of John Eliot, whose pulpit at Roxbury had served as the first mission church in 1645, had so much concern for Indian affairs been shown. The General Court, the following year, then

<!-- p. 61 -->

set up a town at Wnahktutook, where six square miles and the full rights of Englishmen were granted to the native inhabitants. When four white families were chosen to settle with these Indians, the town was incorporated as Stockbridge (1739), and the original natives were later to be known as Stockbridge Indians. It was with these people that Sergeant soon built his reputation as a missionary: amongst them he learnt the Algonquian tongue.[^003-note164]

On the western frontier Sergeant did not gain great success (in spite of frequent long trips to the Susquehanna River in New York). Only at Stockbridge did his mission work thrive. It was there in 1739 that he married Abigail Williams, daughter of Ephraim Williams, a distant cousin of Edwards. There he built a house (which still stands) well-removed from the Indian town. Sergeant combined missionary zeal with the comforts of Berkshire country life. He was, at the same time, the only man to whom Brainerd could then turn. No other person had by 1743 known nine years of missionary life. None had given that much time to the "Moheekanneeus" dialect, or had translated into it passages from Scripture, prayers, and Isaac Watt's *Catechism for Children*.[^003-note165]

As early as 1737 Sergeant had baptized the sachem Yokun and fifty of his followers, and so had paved the way. (When Brainerd later got to Kaunaumeek, his first mission station twenty miles to the west of Stockbridge, he found that "prejudices" against Christianity had already been removed by Sergeant's work.) It was, however, with little hope that Brainerd on the last day of March, 1743, rode into Stockbridge, intending to study the Indian language and to assist Sergeant in his task. Just a year had gone by since he had started the third book of his diary, while living at Ripton with Jedediah Mills. Since then he had visited close to forty towns and had delivered countless sermons; his skill in itinerancy was now well established. But his spirits were not high; he still looked upon himself as a probationer, so that without Sergeant he might have faltered at the start. It was Sergeant who inspired him to found his Indian School at Kaunaumeek, where John Wauwaupeguunnaunt—a Stockbridge Christian—served as master. Through this Indian, who also acted as an interpreter, Brainerd learned to pray with his people in their language and to translate psalms into their tongue.

<!-- p. 62 -->

Later, in other regions, Brainerd's knowledge of Algonquian did him little good. It could not be used to win over the Iroquois on the Susquehanna. But there, although he keenly felt his failure, his efforts inspired others. Eleazer Wheelock (1711–1779), to whom Brainerd sent a copy of his diary (see Related Correspondence), was one of these. Wheelock's determination to propagate the faith among the Iroquois was greater than that of any other figure of the time. Inspired by Brainerd's example, he founded in 1748 a boarding school for Iroquois and whites at Lebanon, Connecticut, where in time he accepted two Delawares from New Jersey (sent by John Brainerd).[^003-note166] Later the school was moved to Hanover, New Hampshire, where in 1770 Wheelock founded Dartmouth College as well.[^003-note167] But his effort on behalf of the Indians came to very little. The Indian school declined as Dartmouth College grew. Wheelock soon discovered, as had Brainerd, that the native scholars were likely to die of disease. Such had been the case in the Indian College at Harvard the century before, where the only graduate died within a year after taking his degree. Still, the desire to educate Indians had been strong from the start; of the funds spent on missionary activities in the colonial period, a high percentage went to education. Brainerd, as the diary shows, spent as much time educating his people as he did in catechizing them, and the motive was not exclusively religious. New Englanders had commonly held that the education of the Indian would improve his character, as with whites, and that religion in the process would benefit as well.[^003-note168] It was hoped that educated Indians would go out as teachers and ministers to other Indians; but it was also hoped that the educated red man would improve society as a whole, and to this end Wheelock had founded his school. To this end he had followed Brainerd's lead.

For the founding of Dickinson's Princeton, Brainerd had provided the perfect model of scholarship combined with evangelical zeal. For the founding of Wheelock's Dartmouth, his example continued to inspire an educational effort. Yale's outcast had not,

<!-- p. 63 -->

of course, set out to be concerned with the founding of sister institutions. As the diary shows, Brainerd had resented institutional life from the start of his freshman year. More than that, he had suffered from the imposition of institutional rules and regulations. But he was, above all, a scholar—a scholar by profession and a missionary by default: and he was vividly aware of the colonists' need for learning. In this regard, his example as an educator has had far more lasting effects than his effort to make Christians out of natives. Both Dickinson and Wheelock owed him a great deal.

#### Confidants

In Brainerd's personal life, however, Wheelock seems not to have played a major part, although he did on occasion give the younger man advice and concerned himself closely with Brainerd's career.[^003-note169] In the personal sphere it was John Brainerd, more than anyone else, who prevailed. To no other person did David in writing reveal his thoughts so openly, as the letters to John at college clearly show. In the last days of his life David is reported to have told Jerusha Edwards that he was willing to part with her, with his friends, and even with his brother John, although he loved him "the best of any creature living."[^003-note170] It was John who brought David's diaries to Northampton just before the end. After David's death it was John who carried on the work of the mission known as Bethel, at Cranbury (old form, Cranberry), New Jersey.

Although John persevered in this job, he seems also to have shared the doubts and struggles of David. Indeed, their common melancholia may have formed a bond between them. Like David, John alludes in his diaries to ill health: and he appears to have been subject—like his brother—to severe mental depression. Of an entry in John's diary for August 27, 1749, where it is written, "felt very poorly, not able to sit up," Thomas Brainerd has made the following observations: "These frequent allusions to ill health are remarkable and painful in a young man of twenty-eight. He shared, we fear, in the feeble constitution that carried his brother David to the grave at twenty-nine, Nehemiah at thirty-two, Israel at twenty-three, and his sister, Jerusha Spencer, at thirty-four.

<!-- p. 64 -->

Though he himself reached sixty, his whole life seems to have been a struggle with physical infirmity. It must, however, be confessed that in the whole Brainerd family for two hundred years there has been a tendency to a morbid depression, akin to hypochondria."[^003-note171]

John entered Yale in 1742 and was graduated in 1746, when he was twenty-six years old. Because he came as a freshman the year of the Whittelsey affair, he must have felt deeply the manner in which his brother had been treated. But he did not abandon his goals. With his brother's moral support, fully expressed in David's letters, he went on with his studies. Indeed, the letters are of great interest not only because they show how much the elder brother cared for the younger but also because they show how readily David was able to "unburden" himself to John, how much franker he could be about his feelings than is evident in the text of the diary. Written in April and December of 1743, and in December of 1745, the letters reveal a deep concern for John's welfare ("Dear brother, may the God of all grace comfort your heart and succeed your studies, and make you an instrument of good to his people in your day") combined with a profound sense of despair ("The whole world appears to me like a huge vacuum, a vast empty space, where nothing desirable or, at least, satisfactory can possibly be derived").[^003-note172]

Although John throughout the diary remains in the background, he is a major figure. David thought him the only person qualified to carry on with the mission when his own health had failed. Yet John, only twenty-seven when his brother was dying, must have been a source of great anxiety to all, especially to himself. He was without experience—either as a minister or as a missionary. He had not been exposed to Indian life, had no knowledge of a tribal tongue, and could not have had a clear idea of what he was taking on. Nor is it clear why David was so eager to have his brother take his place: John might suffer the same hardships from which he himself was dying. Or did David feel that the hard work had been done and that John's job was simply to carry on? In any event, Brainerd wrote in his diary, April 13, 1747: "Assisted in examining my brother" by the New York Presbytery, for licensure; and the April 14 entry reads: "This

<!-- p. 65 -->

day my brother went to my people."[^003-note173] Certainly for Dickinson, Burr, and Edwards the ultimate success or failure of the Bethel enterprise depended upon John, and the authorities in Scotland placed all their hopes on this "pious and ingenious youth" whom they praised for "diligence and success in his mission."[^003-note174] But the enterprise at Bethel was doomed. Incoming white settlers were determined to push out the surviving Indians and take their land. Although an effort was made to secure fresh land in New York, under a scheme to which Edwards gave great support, nothing came of the plan, and the Bethel mission, to which David Brainerd had devoted his short life, and to which John gave all the energy at his command, dwindled away.

This end, however, had been long in the making. Until the time of Robert Morris, who after 1738 was appointed chief justice, Indian land titles had been respected in New Jersey. But Morris having got from the proprietors a title to large holdings, began to treat Indian titles as a nullity, starting actions of ejectment against large numbers. Through legal technicalities he was able to drive from their fields and farms the Indians of the colony, and eventually those at Bethel as well.[^003-note175] Of these events Edwards at the time remarked: "Mr. Morris, the chief justice of the province, … is suing the Indians for their lands under pretext of a will made by their former king, which was undoubtedly forged. However, he is a man of such craft and influence that it is not known how the matter will issue."[^003-note176]

For these reasons John listened favorably to suggestions for removal to another district. Edwards, distressed by John's plight, pressed hard in the spring of 1753 for the prospect of his going to Onohguanga (now Unadilla) on the upper reaches of the Susquehanna in New York. But the Correspondents for the Society failed to act, so that Edwards then observed: "Probably, if the removal cannot be brought about the next year, it never will be."[^003-note177] Another effort was made to buy for Indian settlement a tract of

<!-- p. 66 -->

land of more than four thousand acres in New Jersey. The Society in Scotland endorsed the proposition—voting a good deal of money for the purpose; but this project also ultimately failed.

By 1754, therefore, the prospects for the future were dim. Bethel, which David had procured by paying a debt of the Indians amounting to some ninety pounds, was now threatened, and on May 7, 1755, John was dismissed from his post. It was later argued in Edinburgh that because the Bethel Indians had parted with their lands, and because the Indians in the "back part of the country" were up in arms after General Edward Braddock's defeat (July 9, 1755), that John could not open a new mission. It was further agreed that William Tennent would now and then visit John's former congregation, "catechizing their children, and sometimes … to administer the sacrament of the Lord's Supper to them."[^003-note178]

John, of course, was deeply hurt by his abrupt dismissal, which he thought premature. "I am still in a great plunge," he wrote to Eleazer Wheelock; "I hope I am desirous to know the will of God, but am at a great loss."[^003-note179] Edwards reacted with the deepest concern. Of the action taken by the Correspondents, he wrote to William McCulloch in Scotland: "I cannot say I am fully satisfied with their conduct in doing this so hastily, nor do I pretend to know so much concerning the reasons of their conduct as to have sufficient grounds positively to condemn their proceedings."[^003-note180] But there was, in truth, little that could be done to save John's job. The Correspondents, unable to purchase land on which the Indians might settle, simply could not keep a missionary. Plans were later made to buy land for the Indians near New Brunswick, and in June, 1756, John was reinstated; but the scheme failed and he was dismissed again in September of the following year, having briefly taken charge of the church at Newark—lately served by Aaron Burr. When in 1758 Edwards became President of Princeton and the post at Stockbridge fell empty, it was offered to John. He did not, however, accept.

<!-- p. 67 -->

The final years of John's life were not happy. The death of his wife in 1757 was followed by the deaths of two of his three children. In the summer of 1758 he went briefly to the northern frontier as chaplain of the expedition to Crown Point against the French. The return to civilian life found him again settled as minister at Newark, having been asked once more to resume his mission, which had now been removed to Brotherton. To the end of his life he held on to the remnant of the flock which had originally come to him from his brother. The Synod of New York and Philadelphia continued up to 1780 to vote that "the interest on the Indian fund be paid to Mr. Brainerd for his services among the Indians."[^003-note181] Before he died in 1781 he had established an Indian school and had encouraged Wheelock with the founding of Dartmouth College.

Neither the Scottish Society nor the Synod, however, seemed able to assume responsibility for the Bethel congregation after John had gone. By 1802 only eighty-five Indians remained, and that year they were required to leave for western New York. Along the way, it is said, they passed the night at Cranbury, sleeping on the land once occupied by Bethel, where David Brainerd had established them. According to one witness: "When the Delawares emigrated to Oneida in 1802 or 1804 they passed my residence …. They had twelve wagons for their baggage and those too feeble to journey on foot."[^003-note182] But David, had he lived, could not have prevented this end, no more than could John, who had done all that he could to preserve the Bethel mission. Whether or not John had sworn an oath to do so—before his dying brother—cannot be established, although in David's last days he made two trips to be by his side.

When in April of 1747 the brothers had parted at Elizabethtown, neither then knew that he would see the other only twice more. Nor did they know in parting that this trip to New England would be David's last. Riding slowly on horseback David reached Northampton at the end of May. He rested there until June 9, and then started out for Boston, accompanied by Jerusha Edwards. In July, with his brother Israel and Jerusha riding beside him, he returned to Northampton. He was, according to

<!-- p. 68 -->

John's account, "on his return from Boston to New Jersey, detained by the increase of his disorder."[^003-note183] There is, however, nothing in the diary to suggest that David thought he would reach Bethel once more, for the doctors at Boston had told him that the end was near. Indeed, throughout his stay in the city David had been given up for dead several times; only through a last remission was he able to endure the five days' ride with Israel and Jerusha back to the Edwards house.

This final phase of Brainerd's life, naturally enough, has given rise to much interest, mainly because of Jerusha. From June, 1747, until the following October, when David died, she rarely left his side. But in reading the diary, the part that Jerusha played can only be guessed at, in spite of the temptation to put a romance at the center. Although Field remarks that the two "had anticipated great happiness in married life,"[^003-note184] there is no direct reference to Jerusha throughout the diary. Unless Edwards has suppressed references to his daughter, Brainerd does not mention her name. When toward the end he is brought to the "gates of death" in Boston, and remarks that "divers times in this season my friends gathered round my bed to see me breathe my last," Jerusha is not singled out. On his return to Northampton, "extremely tired and faint on the road," he does not mention Jerusha, who had ridden with him. And in the final entry, where he writes that he is willing to commit to God his dearest friends and even his "absent brother" [^003-note185], there is no mention of Jerusha.[^003-note186]

Edwards never says, furthermore, that the couple were engaged; there is no hint on his part that the friendship ever developed into a romance. Even more curious, Edwards is reluctant to mention Jerusha; until the final pages her name and sex are withheld. It was agreed, Edwards wrote of Brainerd's final trip to Boston, that "one of this family should go with him, and be helpful to him in his weak and low state;"[^003-note187] but the "one of this family," Jerusha, is not singled out either by gender or name. Only toward the end is she identified; but the origin of the friendship is never revealed.

<!-- p. 69 -->

Because there is nothing either in Edwards' or Brainerd's text that tells us when or where the friendship began, we can only guess at its beginnings. Perhaps it started during commencement week, 1743, when Brainerd's classmates gathered to take their degrees. The only bright spot in the events of that week may have been the meeting with Jerusha for the first time. We cannot be sure that she attended; there is no recorded evidence to say that Edwards' second daughter accompanied her father to New Haven that week. But she may have been there; for Edwards was known to take on trips one or another of his daughters, seated on a pillion behind his saddle. Jerusha would have been fourteen years old, which was not then considered too young for serious courtship. Whether or not Brainerd actively courted her that year or in the years that followed cannot, however, be known; we see the two together for the first time, in June, 1747, on David's arrival at the Edwards house.

One is tempted to imagine the couple when they first set out for Boston (as some biographers have done), hoping for a recovery from illness, making plans for the future, and romantically happy. There is, however, no romance in the text. What one finds instead is a dying man attended by a loyal companion. Edwards quotes from two letters that Jerusha wrote in Boston, both of which vividly depict Brainerd's condition. She describes him in one as "very ill with a violent fever, and extreme pain in his head and breast, and, at turns, delirious."[^003-note188] In these letters we hear the voice of a conscientious person who is also a keen observer, but in neither letter can one find a hint of romance. Moreover, one is hard put to know how Brainerd felt about Jerusha. Unless two messages to anonymous recipients were addressed to Jerusha, we have no proof that he even so much as penned a note to her.

Of the letters preserved in the *Life*, one is described as a note that Brainerd wrote to a "special friend," dated July 31, 1744. In it the missionary condemns himself for his failings and decries the wilderness life. He then goes on to say: "It would be very refreshing to me to see you here in this desert; especially in my weak disconsolate hours." The letter concludes with words that anticipate his final remarks to Jerusha at Northampton: "But I think I could be content never to see you or any of my friends

<!-- p. 70 -->

again in this world, if God would bless my labors here to the conversion of the poor Indians." He also declares: "I have much that I could willingly communicate to you, which I must omit, till Providence gives us leave to see each other."[^003-note189] However, it cannot be known whether or not the letter was written to Jerusha. Nor can it be known if some later remarks were intended for her.

On May 22, 1746, Brainerd had experienced what he called "a frame somewhat remarkable," and what he wrote that night may have been addressed to Jerusha. "Farewell, friends and earthly comforts," he exclaimed, "the dearest of them all, the very dearest, if the Lord calls for it; Adieu, Adieu!"[^003-note190] But Edwards put it in the text as part of the diary, and here too the figure of Jerusha can only be surmised. Indeed, the extent to which thoughts of Jerusha came into the manuscript diary at all can only be guessed at.

We learn from Edwards that in the last days at Northampton Jerusha took care of David much of the time. Dr. Mather, the village physician, had told the failing Brainerd that he would not recover, and Jerusha in these final weeks appears to have managed his life. But she knew nothing about tuberculosis—least of all that it was contagious. Brainerd was free to go where he liked, infecting as he went all those with whom he came into contact. Dr. Joseph Pynchon, who had treated him in Boston, knew as much about the disease as anyone in New England; but even he did not know that it was infectious. Whether or not Edwards ever suspected that Jerusha *had* contracted Brainerd's sickness cannot be deduced from the text, although the graphic details of the disease (the diarrhea, the vomiting of pus and blood) must have been her report. Suffice it to say that the two deaths *were* linked in Edwards' mind. "Since this," he wrote, "it has pleased a holy and sovereign God to take away this my dear child by death, on the 14th of February, next following, after a short illness of five days, in the eighteenth year of her age." She was a person, he went on, "of much the same spirit as Mr. Brainerd."[^003-note191] He noted as well that she was "generally esteemed the flower of the family" and that "herein we have a great loss."[^003-note192] Five days after her funeral he delivered a eulogy in which he spoke of her as "my own

<!-- p. 71 -->

dear child"[^003-note193] and expressed his personal feelings more freely than on any other recorded occasion in his ministry. He had her buried next to Brainerd in the town lot, where her stone still guards the slab that marks his grave (see photographs, pp. 72–3).

It was not in Edwards' nature to blame Brainerd for his daughter's death. Nor did he complain of the disruptions that the invalid's presence had brought into family life. Because of Brainerd, daily routine had in every way to be adjusted. The best that the sick man could do, according to medical opinion at the time, was to continue riding, as it was believed that such activity would prolong his life. Why the doctors held to this remedy cannot be fully explained, but the trek between saddle and bed became a ritual part of the Edwards house. Near the end, bedside care was continuously required; pans had frequently to be brought back and forth. But we shall never know, oddly enough, who had invited the missionary to come. Did the invitation come from Edwards, from Jerusha, or had Brainerd invited himself?

### 4. Notes on the Text and Manuscript

A question that has long been asked is to what extent the *Life of Brainerd* may with fairness be called a "biography" or even a "work" of Edwards? Because it consists of selections from the diary, which in turn are accompanied by Edwards' comments, the text is essentially Brainerd's. For this reason the 1808 Worcester edition of Edwards' works includes only the last part of the diary, together with Edwards' "Reflections." The editor defends his omissions on the grounds that the text "consists almost wholly of extracts from Mr. Brainerd's Diary, and his own words."
