## Related Correspondence

<!-- p. 555 -->

<!-- p. 556 -->

<!-- p. 557 -->

### Introduction

Seven letters composed between 1743 and 1747 have bearing upon issues raised in Edwards' *Life of Brainerd*. Five were written by Brainerd, one by his brother John, and one by Edwards. All shed light on Brainerd's activities in the last four years of his life.

The first, sent from New Haven to an unidentified correspondent under the dateline May 21, 1743, is now held in the Beinecke collection at Yale; it is a rare example of Brainerd's hand and epistolary style in the period following his expulsion from college. In it he expresses his fondness for the recipient, with whose trials he sympathizes, and gives an account of recent events. Of special concern, however, is the date.For a discussion of the date of the letter and of the identity of the unknown correspondent, see the Rev. Arthur Bennett, letter to Marjorie G. Wynne, June 25, 1965, Beinecke collection. On May 21, 1743, Brainerd was not at New Haven but at Kaunaumeeks, having arrived there the previous March. On May 30 he left Kaunaumeek for Newark, New Jersey, which he reached June 2, and on his return called at New Haven June 6 to seek reconciliation with the college authorities, arriving back at Kaunaumeek June 12. Unless he sent the letter by courier to be posted at New Haven, May 21, he misdated the heading, as he did some of his other correspondence.

A more likely date would be May of the year before. Throughout the spring of 1742, after his dismissal from college, Brainerd wandered about Connecticut. On May 19 he was at Millington, and on May 28 at New Haven, where he spent some time. His reference to the college as a "sorrowful place" and to "our separate meeting" as a "sorrowful case" fits the prevailing conditions at New Haven, where in the wake of Davenport's attack on Noyes some sixty townsmen had on May 5, 1742, set up a Separatist church. The tone of Brainerd's remarks would best fit this period of turmoil; for by 1743 the new meeting had settled down.

<!-- p. 558 -->

It should also be recalled that one of the three charges leading to Brainerd's expulsion, a charge he denied, was that of attending a Separatist meeting. But it is clear from the letter that he was intimate with this group, and it is hardly likely that a year later he would still want to associate with it, for by then his antagonism to all forms of enthusiasm had led him to shun divisiveness.

The identity of the unknown correspondent, who appears to have been engaged in ministerial duties and to have undergone trials in his work, has also to be taken into account. For lack of evidence, certain identification is not possible; but because the letter reflects an intimate association between writer and receiver, the most likely recipient is Samuel Buell, who with David Youngs and Brainerd had formed the enthusiast group at Yale. The letter tells us that the recipient lived in poor lodgings and that Brainerd was concerned about his "weakly" state, factors which point to Buell, an itinerant preacher at the time who was also ill. Brainerd also mentions "your dear brother," a possible reference to Peter Buell, Samuel's younger half-brother, then a boy preparing to join the class of 1749.

Mentioned as well are Job Prudden and Elihu Spencer, who were then close to Brainerd. Prudden, a member of Brainerd's college class, would still have been a junior in May of 1742. Later he was pastor of the second church at Milford, to which he was asked in 1747 because of his Separatist reputation. (He married in 1750 Esther Sherman, who is mentioned in Edwards' letter to John Brainerd as a person with whom David corresponded.) Spencer, class of 1746, was about to enter college when Brainerd was expelled. He was Brainerd's second cousin, childhood friend, and the third member of the family to become a missionary. (Together with Job Strong he founded a mission to the Six Nations, for which he prepared during the winter of 1747–48 with John Brainerd and the following summer with Edwards.)Dexter, *Biographical Sketches*, 1, pp. 742–43; 2, pp. 89–92. JE wrote to John Erskine, October 14, 1748: "The commissioners in Boston of the Corporation in London for the Propagation of the Gospel among the Indians in N. England and Parts Adjacent, a little before Mr. David Brainerd went to Boston, the summer before his death, had received a sum of money from the estate left by the famous Dr. Williams, for the maintenance of two missionaries among the Six Nations: And having entertained a very great esteem of Mr. Brainerd from the opportunity they had of acquaintance with him while in Boston, they committed to him the affair of finding and recommending the persons proper to be employed in this business. Accordingly he after much deliberation recommended one Mr. Spencer belonging to Haddam, his native town, and Mr. Strong belonging to this town, Northampton: who are undoubtedly well qualified persons, of good abilities and learning, and of pious dispositions. The commissioners, on his recommendation, accepted these persons; and after Mr. Brainerd's death sent to 'em; and they went down to Boston and accepted the mission. But the commissioners did not think proper immediately to send 'em forth among the Six Nations; but ordered them to go and live, during the winter, in New Jersey with Mr. John Brainerd, among the Christian Indians, there to follow their studies and get acquaintance with the manners and customs of Indians; and in the spring to go with Mr. Brainerd to Susquehanna to instruct the Indians on that river, before they went to the Six Nations. Accordingly they went and lived in New Jersey; but were discouraged as to their intended journey to Susquehanna; for they understood that the Susquehanna Indians greatly objected against entertaining missionaries without the consent of the Six Nations (to whom they are subject and of whom it seemed they stand in great fear) and insisted that the missionaries should go to the Six Nations first. Therefore in the spring Messrs. Spencer and Strong returned to Boston for new orders from the commissioners, who saw cause to order them to come and live at my house 'till the time of an appointed interview of the Governors of Boston and New York, with the Chiefs of the Six Nations at Albany, in the latter part of summer." Andover coll.

<!-- p. 559 -->

At the close of the letter are references to persons who also require identification, notably Abigail Horton. Born Abigail Howell, she was the wife of Simon Horton (second cousin of Azariah), then pastor of the Presbyterian church in Connecticut Farms, near Elizabeth.Ibid., Dexter, 1, pp. 427–28. Brainerd on his travels in New Jersey had sought out Horton (an active "New Side" minister) and felt especially close to his wife. But to whom Brainerd refers in mentioning "my mother" as a living person and "my sister Sarah" cannot be so easily explained. He may have had in mind someone to whom he looked as an adopted mother. The nomenclature "sister" he habitually used in the broadest sense, referring also in this letter to Abigail Horton as a "sister in Christ."

The second letter, sent to Ebenezer Pemberton from the Forks of the Delaware on November 5, 1744, was published as "A Narrative relating to the Indian Affairs," and bound with Pemberton's sermon given at Brainerd's ordination (Boston, printed by Rogers and Fowle for J. Pemberton, 1744). Because Ebenezer Pemberton wanted to publicize Brainerd's efforts, he had solicited the letter, which with the sermon he inscribed "To the Right Honorable The Marquis of Lothian, President, and the rest of the members of the incorporated Society in Scotland for Propagating Christian Knowledge." As head Correspondent for the Society, Pemberton had wasted no time seeing the *Narrative* into

<!-- p. 560 -->

print. (The ordination, at Newark, took place June 12, 1744.) Because Edwards in the *Life* refers to the *Narrative* six times, it is clearly of such importance as to demand inclusion within the present volume.

Of similar importance is Brainerd's letter to John Sergeant, written "in greatest haste" at Woodbury, Connecticut, March 15, 1745. First printed in William B. O. Peabody's *Life of David Brainerd* (pp. 319–321), it briefly recounts Brainerd's work on the Susquehanna and Delaware rivers, inquires about plans for an Indian school at Stockbridge, and informs Sergeant that the proceeds from the sale of two kettles should be used for the school. "I sold my teakettle to Mr. Jo. Woodbridge, and an iron kettle to Mr. Timothy Woodbridge," Brainerd wrote, "both which amounted to something more than four pounds, which I ordered them to pay to you for the school."

The Woodbridge brothers, Joseph (b. 1707) and Timothy (b. 1709), were sons of the Rev. John Woodbridge (Harvard class of 1694) and of Jemima Eliot (a granddaughter of the "Apostle Eliot"), of West Springfield, where in 1718 the Rev. Woodbridge was killed by a falling tree. Timothy, who in 1736 married Abigail Day, went early to Stockbridge as an assistant to John Sergeant. Later he was Superintendent of Indian Affairs and judge of the Court in Hampshire County. He is not to be confused with his cousin of the same name (Yale class of 1732), who was minister at Hatfield. Joseph, who in 1730 married Elizabeth Barnard, soon joined Timothy at the Stockbridge mission, later was Judge of Probate, and outlived his brother (who died in 1775) by several years. Both brothers built in Stockbridge, where they added in the course of time to the articles bought from Brainerd in 1745.

Brainerd tells Sergeant as well that his funds are low, that he was forced to kill his mare and has not the money to replace her, that he hopes to raise money to support a missionary companion, and that his blankets are to be traded for deer skins, which should be sent as a gift either to Samuel Hopkins or Joseph Bellamy. The letter, in short, is a financial report combined with charitable bequests.

We know from the diary that on March 7, 1745, Brainerd had set out from Crossweeksung for a five weeks' journey to New England, where he hoped "to raise some money among Christian

<!-- p. 561 -->

friends, in order to support a colleague with me in the wilderness," and that this was the "principal concern" he had in taking the journey. Edwards tells us that the trip took Brainerd various "to parts of Connecticut," where he met "a number of ministers" whom he hoped would support his cause (see above, p. 290); so that the letter to Sergeant from Woodbury (now Washington, Connecticut) may be seen as part of this effort, in that it frankly and directly states Brainerd's needs.

Two letters bearing on Brainerd's public *Journal* (1746) have also been included in the present volume. One was written to Eleazer Wheelock, December 30, 1745, and the other to the Philadelphia publisher William Bradford, September 20, 1746. The first is extant in a copy not in Brainerd's hand; both are held in the manuscript collection at Yale.

The letter to Wheelock was sent to the recipient along with a manuscript of the journal, the original of which had been sent abroad. "The large manuscript that accompanies this letter," Brainerd wrote, "is a copy of a journal I lately sent home to Scotland." He continued: "The pressure of my business is such that I was obliged to employ another hand to transcribe it for me, except the general remarks, at the latter end, which I wrote myself." He then described the transcription, for which he apologized. The copyist, he explained, has not been careful "to preserve the printing and distinct paragraphs," and has "wholly omitted" certain sentences, which have since been restored as addenda on the last page.Of special interest here is that Brainerd's description of the copy perfectly fits the manuscript now held at The Connecticut Historical Society. That manuscript, with the exception of the general remarks and the addenda, is also not in Brainerd's hand. What the letter reveals is that the copy of the journal sent to Wheelock and the manuscript now in Hartford are one and the same. Brainerd hoped, nevertheless, that Wheelock would be "able to read it" as documentary proof of a worthy cause. "I doubt not by that time you have read my journal through," he wrote, "you'll be more sensible of the need I stand in of a companion in travel than ever you was before." Wheelock is further informed that Brainerd hoped to "collect something" for support of such a colleague "among religious people in one place and another," having recently been encouraged in this effort by "Mr. Ebenezer Mills," "Mr. Barker," "Mr. Williams of Lebanon," and "my friend Sam Rockwell." The project might be helped

<!-- p. 562 -->

along, he suggested, if Wheelock were to put in a letter his own estimate of potential support and send a copy to Pemberton.

Of this list of well-wishers Ebenezer Mills was probably the least reliable. Eight years older than Brainerd, he is said to have studied theology with his brother Jedidiah, with whom Brainerd had lived after the expulsion from Yale. At the time of Brainerd's letter Mills was settled over the parish of Turkey Hills (now East Granby), where he had been called in 1741. His tenure, however, was not a happy one; after prolonged controversy he was dismissed. He afterwards settled in Sandisfield, Massachusetts, where he gradually went insane and mysteriously disappeared.Dexter, *Biographical Sketches, 1*, pp. 607–08.

Nehemiah Barker, mentioned after Mills, also had difficulties fitting into a settled church. Yale class of 1742, he was slightly younger than Brainerd, having been born in 1719 or 1720. The first notice of him after graduation is the advice of the Fairfield East Association to the congregation in Unity, now Trumbull, to apply to "Mr. Barker of Lebannon or thereabout" as a candidate for settlement. He was invited to supply that pulpit, and preached for some months, but did not receive a call to settle. In December of 1745, when Brainerd wrote to Wheelock, Barker was preaching to the parish in Woodstock, but he did not accept the call to settle. The following year he went to preach at South Killingly, but the spread of Separate principles so weakened the enterprise that he sought dismissal after nine years.Ibid., *1*, pp. 700–01.

The most formidable name on the list, "Mr. Williams of Lebanon," may have been some help to Brainerd. Solomon Williams (1700–1776), cousin of Edwards, was a life-long friend of Wheelock, with whom he had held prayer meetings. By more ardent New Lights his doctrine was regarded as Arminian; yet he opposed the anti-New Light legislation of 1742. Together with Wheelock he condemned Davenport's excesses, but joined Edwards on the matter of the Half-Way Covenant. From 1722, when he first began to preach at Lebanon, his stature in Connecticut had steadily increased, and when Brainerd at the close of the letter asked Wheelock to "give my duty to Mr. Williams," he knew that an influential voice might well be on his side.Shipton, *Sibley's Harvard Graduates, 6*, pp. 352–61.

The reference to "my friend Sam Rockwell" is of special interest,

<!-- p. 563 -->

not only because Rockwell is the only person described as a "friend," but also because he is the only person not a fellow minister. Born January 19, 1728, the son of Joseph Rockwell of Windsor, Samuel had matured under the ministry of Timothy Edwards. He had also listened to Whitefield and had heard the younger Edwards preach. (It may have been through Edwards that he and Brainerd met.) At the time of Brainerd's letter Rockwell was seventeen. Known for his piety, "vigorous personality," and remarkable ability to secure "united action" amongst fellow men, he was also endowed with "great physical strength." In short, he could be trusted to muster support. Later he settled Colebrook, whose military company he commanded during the Revolutionary War.Henry R. Stiles, *The History and Genealogies of Ancient Windsor, Connecticut*, 1635–1891 (2 vols., Hartford, Lockwood and Brainard Co., 1892), 2, pp. 651–52.

Brainerd's closing request, that "my brother Mason" be allowed to read the journal, refers to Elijah Mason (Yale class of 1744), another friend who, like Mills and Barker, was highly unstable in his ways. Whether or not he showed signs of instability a year out of college is hard to say. Brainerd did not seek his support, but simply asked that Wheelock show him the journal; "for I han't time to write to him." Licensed by the Hartford North Association only three days before Brainerd died, Mason preached from 1748 in what is now Marlborough, Connecticut, but fell into intemperate habits and was deposed from the ministry in 1761. Later he reformed and was installed at Chester, where from 1767 he preached for the last three years of his life.Dexter, *Biographical Sketches, 1*, p. 765.

The letter to William Bradford is self-explanatory and needs little comment. In it Brainerd is concerned with the printing of his journal, especially the appendix, and asks Bradford to alter scriptural citations on the title pages of both parts. The letter shows the close attention to detail with which Brainerd saw the journal through the press. Bradford, only three years earlier, had established his business at "The Sign of the Bible," hoping to gain a reputation independent of his grandfather (the famous pioneer printer of the middle colonies whose name he bore), and the printing of Brainerd's journal helped to get him under way. From 1748 he printed a number of Gilbert Tennent's sermons, hoping to attract similar treatises, but politics soon pushed theology aside;

<!-- p. 564 -->

he became the "patriot printer" of 1776, rose to the rank of colonel in Washington's army, and was badly wounded at Princeton, whence Brainerd had written in 1746.Isaiah Thomas, *History of Printing in America* (2 vols., Worcester, 1810), 2. p. 564.

Two letters not written by David Brainerd, one from John Brainerd to Ebenezer Pemberton (June 23, 1747), the other from Edwards to John Brainerd (December 14, 1747), complete the collection of related correspondence. The first points to the link between the Brainerd's work and colonial expansion, the second to the difficulties Edwards faced when he came to write the *Life.*

John's letter to Pemberton, first printed in Philip Doddridge's *Abridgment of Brainerd's Journal* (London, 1748, pp. 112–113),Reprinted in Thomas Brainerd, *Life of John Brainerd*, pp. 116–18. is a brief comment on conditions at Bethel the spring before David died. Doddridge put it in the appendix, along with a letter from Pemberton to the President of the Society in Scotland (July 21, 1747), assuring the Scots that in spite of David's illness his work would be carried on. Because Pemberton feared that on David's death funds might be withdrawn, he had enclosed John's letter with his own. "That you may have a clearer view of the circumstances of the Indians under Mr. Brainerd's care," he wrote, "I have enclosed a letter I lately received from his brother, who, as I before observed, officiates in Mr. Brainerd's room while he continues disabled by sickness." He further explained:

> Mr. Brainerd has indeed been confined by sickness for a long time, and is yet in a low and dangerous state of health occasioned by his incessant fatigues and travels in the prosecution of his mission. But lest the Indian service should suffer during his sickness, he has procured his brother (a pious and ingenious young candidate for the ministry) to reside among the Indians, who meets with great acceptance and success among them. Whether Mr. Brainerd will ever recover seems as yet uncertain; he has now for several months been hovering upon the borders of the grave; but, even in his low estate, has been doing more than could possibly have been expected in the service in which he is engaged. If it should please God to take him out of the world, it would be, I had almost said, an irreparable loss, but I recall that word; with God is "the residue of the spirit" Malachi 2:15.

<!-- p. 565 -->

Doddridge, as an epilogue to both letters, added a "Postscript" reporting David's death; but at the same time he assured the world "that his brother Mr. John Brainerd succeeds in the honorable employment of missionary, at the new Indian town which they have properly enough named Bethel, where he bids fair to follow the footsteps of his deceased brother, not only in his piety, but in his abilities, activity, and zeal for the Kingdom of God, and that he meets with great encouragement and acceptance amongst the Indians, whose congregation and English school continue to prosper and increase by newcomers from other Indian countries." Doddridge then expanded on this theme; if the process of "civilizing as well as Christianizing the poor savages of America" is to continue, he went on, the enterprise "may well merit the attention of the public": and he cited the Bethel mission in order to praise "the benefits which, even on political and mercantile considerations, will thereby hereafter accrue to Great Britain"; for "by bringing the Indians to live in a regular way (a difficulty till now thought insurmountable) with fixed habitations and farms, his Majesty may thereby in time have a large addition of settled subjects in America, who may hereafter prove greatly instrumental in the improvement and cultivation of the waste lands there, as also in raising materials thereon for our own commerce and manufactures." The notion that missions should augment imperial policy is even more forcefully put in Doddridge's final appeal, which openly declares that Christianity serves the best interests of colonial expansion:

> It seems therefore to be of no small importance to Great Britain that all possible endeavors be used for the conversion of the Indians, in and bordering on our colonies in America, to the Christian religion, even on the score of mere human policy alone; since by Christianizing of them, their becoming civilized almost naturally follows. Thus the promoting of this excellent work, is, in effect, as much our interest with respect to this world, singly considered, as it is our highest duty and interest with respect to eternity. It is therefore to be hoped that all such as have these united considerations in their sight, will in their several stations, and according to their respective abilities, contribute to strengthen the hands of a Society, which not only supports a great number of schools at home, in the

<!-- p. 566 -->

  Highlands and Isles adjacent, but does likewise use their utmost endeavors to spread the Gospel into the remotest parts of the British Empire.

It has been said of Doddridge that his correspondence is remarkable for "its absence of reserve, and its pervading element of healthy good sense." As one of the leading nonconformists of his day (1702–1751), he was frequently at odds with ecclesiastical authorities, while at the same time he did more than any other man to unite nonconformists and obliterate party lines. His scheme for foreign missions, presented to three different assemblies of ministers in 1741, was the first nonconformist project of its kind; so that his interest in Brainerd can readily be understood. Like Brainerd, he stood midway between Presbyterians and Congregationlists; his zeal for missions knew no bounds. It has also been said of Doddridge that he had "too many irons in the fire," that one project easily gave way to another, the abridgment of Brainerd's journal being one of these.*DNB, 5*, 1063–69. But the value of the Doddridge edition cannot be overstressed, not only because of the letters appended, but also because of the manner in which Brainerd's mission is discussed.

The final item of related correspondence, Edwards' letter to John Brainerd, also serves as a fitting epilogue to the present volume; for it deals with efforts to prepare and promote the *Life*. Written in his own hand, with the address on the reverse of the last sheet, it is held in the Andover Newton Collection of Edwards manuscripts.

Edwards wrote to John, December 14, 1747, determined to publish an "abstract" of his brother's papers. In addition, he wanted help in persuading Governor Belcher to allow the *Life* to be dedicated to him, in order to "make it more taken notice of" and to "do honor to your brother's memory, whom many in his lifetime strove to lay under disgrace." Edwards also wanted John to be courier: "I have sent my letter to the Governor open," he wrote, "that you may see it, but desire you handsomely to seal and deliver it." Belcher, appointed governor of New Jersey only the year before, would add luster to the title page, and Edwards may have hoped that family ties would expedite the matter. Belcher was warmly attached to Elihu Spencer, David's and John's

<!-- p. 567 -->

cousin, of whose Presbyterian Church at Elizabeth he was a member; he was also known to favor the College of New Jersey, to which he later bequeathed a library of 374 volumes.*DAB*, 2, 143–44. But as the matter turned out, he apparently did not want his name linked to one that had lain under disgrace.

Apart from this blatant bid for patronage, what strikes the reader of the letter is how little Edwards knew about the person whose biography he intended to write. He knew little about the family, especially the maternal side. In spite of having pleaded for Brainerd with Yale, he did not know all the facts of the case, which he now asks John to provide, so that a "just, exact and certain account" might be given that will not offend Rector Clapp. Of special concern is a "confession" that David is said to have offered the justice at Hartford the May after his expulsion, about which Edwards suggests that Aaron Burr or Jedediah Mills might provide more facts. In addition, John is asked to bring to Northampton "any other of your brother's papers," and to ask Esther Sherman to send on some of David's letters to her, as she is mentioned in the diary as a correspondent to whom he felt close. But the nature of the correspondence cannot be ascertained. Unless the letter to a "special friend" (Some Further Remains, Pt. IV, No. 4) was addressed to her, none is extant. The eldest child of Nathaniel Sherman of New Haven, and five years older than David, she later married Job Prudden, his college friend, whom she survived by one year.Roy V. Sherman, *The New England Shermans* (Copyright 1974), p. 51.

Edwards in his closing remarks tells John that "Mr. Bromfield" has sent word that the funeral sermon for Brainerd is in the press and that "Maj. Henchman" will publish it without a subscription, referring to Edward Bromfield (1695–1756), Boston merchant known for his New Light sympathies, and to Daniel Henchman (1689–1761), eminent bookseller who also served in the Boston regiment of militia. (Bromfield may have supplied a subvention, his pious son Edward having died of illness the year before.)Thomas Prince, *The Case of Heman Considered. In a sermon occasioned by the death of Mr. Edward Bromfield* (Boston, S. Kneeland, 1756), pp. 30–31; Thomas, *History of Printing*, 2, p. 422. JE relied on Bromfield to handle his affairs. The following summer he wrote to John Erskine, August 31, 1748: "Please to accept of one of my sermons on Mr. Brainerd's death, and also my sermon on Mr. Buell's installment. I desire that for the future your letters to me may be directed to be left with Mr. Edward Bromfield, merchant of Boston, and not with Mr. Prince, who is so forgetful that his care is not to be depended upon." Andover coll. Had

<!-- p. 568 -->

Edwards by then been sent a copy of the sermon, the postscript concludes, he would have sent it on to Belcher. Perhaps John might do the same on receiving his own.JE took a personal interest in promoting not only the Funeral Sermon but also the *Life*. He wrote to John Erskine, May 20, 1749: "I shall send order, to Boston, that one of my books on Mr. Brainerd's life may be sent to you, with this letter; if any of them are ready, as I hope they are or will be very speedily." Andover coll.

#### Brainerd to an Unidentified Correspondent

New Haven, May 21, 1743

Dear Sir,

After my tender and sincere love to you, I having this opportunity of writing to you, though most unworthy, I rejoiced to hear from you. I am obliged to you for your love, although at the hearing of your letter I felt hurt to my heart for you, for you are very near to me. But blessed be God that has made you willing to undergo all what you do for them, dear soul. But I will give you a brief account of what I have felt since I saw you. I have felt for some time very remarkably sweet and spiritual. Oh, I dwelt in the secrets of God's presence. I seemed to abide under the shadow of the Almighty from day to day. I felt what the religion of Christ Jesus is. I felt the most submitted and sweetly swallowed up in the will of the blessed God that it was my meat and drink to do the will of my heavenly father. I prayed always incessantly, and my whole soul searched to acquiesce in the divine will. Oh, sweet resignation! Blessed be God for sweet seasons and for the most pressing trials, for I have had the most pressing trials that ever I endured. It seems to me that my soul trials have been so great that I can't express them. I was almost in despair. I could not see nothing either in heaven or earth that could afford me the least happiness. I was under great temptation. I was tempted to never to pray anymore, but instead of not praying I prayed more than ever, and God seemed to press me down with one hand and hold me up with the other. I could have been glad to unreadable[Yale editor's brackets used throughout.] out of being. I had such an amazing sense of my vileness and unholiness and purity of infinite God and his power and greatness, but my vileness seemed greater than ever, but my unreadable have been and are so great that I can't express them. I

<!-- p. 569 -->

know of no words to do it in, but I han't time to write. But as for religion it is almost gone; as for Christians I can't tell you about them, for my heart breaks sometimes for them. As for college it is a sorrowful place. There is some dear souls, your dear brother and Prudden and Spencer are dear. Christ, we have such dear sweet season to gather to pray, and blessed be God: and as for our separate meeting it is in a sorrowful case, and I feel sometimes as if I should die. But I fully believe there is something that is not right, that I feel sometimes, so it seems to me that I can never go again to meeting, but some time I have felt sweetly there. But your brother will write more full concerning these things. Dear Sir, I entreat your patience, for I feel I am a unreadable vile worm and my trials are so great and present that I can't wait. Oh, if you can pray for me, but I feel unworthy of your prayer, but I long to hear you pray.

It seems to me it would be sweet to join in prayers with you. It has been sweet many a time to pray for you, though in the greatest agonies I have had so great a sense of your work and your own weakness and nothingness and the preciousness of dear immortal souls. I was in a sweet agony for some days for you for heaven blessing until I was so weak in body that I could hardly sit up for a week together. Dear Sir, I believe that the great and blessed God has many blessings for you. Oh, may you approve yourself a disciple of that Master who whilst taken walking here on earth had not where to lay his head but went about doing good. Oh, that you may have his sweet and blessed temper that you may be all love and humble and meek, gentle, peaceable and full of tenderness and have the bowels of Christ for dear souls and be filled with all the fruits of righteousness and true holiness that you may watch in all things, endure afflictions. I do the work of an evangelist. Make full unreadable of thy ministry that you may at last shine as the stars for ever and ever. I long to see you and I am concerned for you about your lodging. Do lodge better if you can. You are very weakly but I must leave you with your God and Father. This from your true, the unworthy sister in Christ, A.H. Abigail Horton.

My mother gives her respects to you. My sister Sarah gives her dear love to you, though you forget her. We all long to see you for now we unreadable your prayers for us all.

D. Brainerd

<!-- p. 570 -->

#### Brainerd to Ebenezer Pemberton

Rev. Sir,

Since you are pleased to require of me some brief and general account of my conduct in the affair of my mission amongst the Indians, the pains and endeavors I have used to propagate Christian knowledge among them, the difficulties I have met with in pursuance of that great work, and the hopeful and encouraging appearances I have observed in any of them, I shall now endeavor to answer your demands by giving a brief but faithful account of the most material things relating to that important affair, with which I have been and am still concerned. And this I shall do with more freedom and cheerfulness both because I apprehend it will be a likely means to give pious persons who are concerned for the kingdom of Christ some just apprehension of the many and great difficulties that attend the propagation of it amongst the poor pagans, and consequently 'tis hopeful will engage their more frequent and fervent prayers to God, that those may be succeeded who are employed in this arduous work: And also because I persuade myself that the tidings of the Gospel's spreading among the poor heathen will be to those who are waiting for the accomplishment of the "glorious things spoken of the city of our God" Psalms 87:3 as "good news from a far country" Proverbs 25:25; and that these will be so far from "despising the day of small things" Zechariah 4:10 that on the contrary the least dawn of encouragement and hope in this important affair will rather inspire their pious breasts with more generous and warm desires that "the kingdoms of this world" Jeremiah 25:26; Matthew 4:8 may speedily become "the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ" Ephesians 5:5.

I shall therefore immediately proceed to the business before me and briefly touch upon the most important matters that have concerned my mission from the beginning to this present time.

On March 15, 1743, I waited on the Correspondents for the Indian mission at New York, and the week following attended their meeting at Woodbridge in New Jersey and was speedily dismissed by them with orders to attempt the instruction of a number of Indians in a place some miles distant from the city of Albany. And on the first day of April following, I arrived among the Indians at a place called by them Kaunaumeek, in the county

<!-- p. 571 -->

of Albany, near about twenty miles distant from the city eastward.

The place as to its situation was sufficiently lonesome and unpleasant, being encompassed with mountains and woods, twenty miles distant from any English inhabitants, six or seven from any Dutch, and more than two from a family that came some time since from the Highlands of Scotland, and had then lived (as I remember) about two years in this wilderness. In this family I lodged about the space of three months, the master of it being the only person with whom I could readily converse in those parts, except my interpreter, others understanding very little English.

After I had spent about three months in this situation, I found my distance from the Indians a very great disadvantage to my work amongst them, and very burdensome to myself, as I was obliged to travel forward and backward almost daily on foot, having no pasture in which I could keep my horse for that purpose, and after all my pains could not be with the Indians in the evening and morning, which were usually the best hours to find them at home, and when they could best attend my instructions.

I therefore resolved to remove and live with or near the Indians, that I might watch all opportunities when they were generally at home and take the advantage of such seasons for their instruction.

Accordingly I removed soon after, and for a time lived with them in one of their wigwams, and not long after built me a small house where I spent the remainder of that year entirely alone, my interpreter (who was an Indian) choosing rather to live in a wigwam among his own countrymen.

This way of living I found attended with many difficulties and uncomfortable circumstances, in a place where I could get none of the necessaries and common comforts of life (no, not so much as a morsel of bread) but what I brought from places fifteen and twenty miles distant, and oftentimes was obliged for some time together to content myself without, for want of an opportunity to procure the things I needed.

But although the difficulties of this solitary way of living are not the least or most inconsiderable (and doubtless are in fact many more and greater to those who experience than they can readily appear to those who only view them at a distance), yet I can truly say that the burden I felt respecting my great work among the

<!-- p. 572 -->

poor Indians, the fear and concern that continually hung upon my spirit lest they should be prejudiced against Christianity, and their minds embittered against me and my labors among them by means of the insinuations of some who (although they are called Christians) seem to have no concern for Christ's kingdom, but had rather (as their conduct plainly discovers) that the Indians should remain heathens, that they may with the more ease cheat and so enrich themselves by them; the burden, I say, the fear and concern I felt in these respects were much more pressing to me than all the difficulties that attended the circumstances of my living.

As to the state or temper of mind in which I found these Indians at my first coming among them, I may justly say it was much more desirable and encouraging than what appears among those who are altogether uncultivated. Their heathenish jealousy and suspicion and their prejudices against Christianity were in a great measure removed by the long continued labors of the Rev. Mr. Sergeant among a number of the same tribe in a place little more than twenty miles distant: by which means these were in some good degree prepared to entertain the truths of Christianity instead of objecting against them and appearing almost entirely untractable, as is common with them at first, and as perhaps these appeared a few years ago. Some of them, at least, appeared very well disposed toward religion, and seemed much pleased with my coming among them.

In my labors with them, in order "to turn them from darkness to light" Acts 26:18, I studied what was most plain and easy and best suited to their capacities, and endeavored to set before them from time to time (as they were able to receive them) the most important and necessary truths of Christianity; such as most immediately concerned their speedy conversion to God, and such as I judged had the greatest tendency (as means) to effect that glorious change in them. But especially I made it the scope and drift of all my labors to lead them into a thorough acquaintance with these two things.

First, the sinfulness and misery of the estate they were naturally in: the evil of their hearts, the pollution of their natures, the heavy guilt they were under, and their exposedness to everlasting punishment; as also their utter inability to save themselves either from their sins or from those miseries which are the

<!-- p. 573 -->

just punishment of them; and their unworthiness of any mercy at the hand of God on account of anything they themselves could do to procure his favor, and consequently their extreme need of Christ to save them.

And secondly, I frequently endeavored to open to them the fullness, all-sufficiency, and freeness of that redemption which the Son of God has wrought out by his obedience and sufferings for perishing sinners; how this provision he had made was suited to all their wants, and how he called and invited them to accept of everlasting life freely, notwithstanding all their sinfulness, inability, unworthiness, etc.

After I had been with the Indians several months, I composed sundry forms of prayer adapted to their circumstances and capacities, which with the help of my interpreter I translated into the Indian language, and soon learned to pronounce their words so as to pray with them in their own tongue. I also translated sundry Psalms into their language, and soon after we were able to sing in the worship of God.

When my people had gained some acquaintance with many of the truths of Christianity to that they were capable of receiving and understanding many others which at first could not be taught them, by reason of their ignorance of those that were necessary to be previously known, and upon which others depended, I then gave them an historical account of God's dealings with his ancient professing people, the Jews: some of the rites and ceremonies they were obliged to observe, as their sacrifices, etc., and what these were designed to represent to them, as also some of the surprising miracles God wrought for their salvation while they trusted in him, and the sore punishments he sometimes brought upon them when they forsook and sinned against him. Afterwards I proceeded to give them a relation of the birth, life, miracles, sufferings, death, and resurrection of Christ, as well as his ascension and the wonderful effusion of the Holy Spirit consequent thereupon.

And having thus endeavored to prepare the way by such a general account of things, I next proceeded to read and expound to them the Gospel of St. Matthew (at least the substance of it) in course, wherein they had a more distinct and particular view of what they had before some general notion of.

These expositions I attended almost every evening when there

<!-- p. 574 -->

was any considerable number of them at home, except when I was obliged to be absent myself in order to learn the Indian language with the Rev. Mr. Sergeant. Besides these means of instruction there was likewise an English school constantly kept by my interpreter among the Indians, which I used frequently to visit in order to give the children and young people some proper instructions and serious exhortations suited to their age.

The degree of knowledge to which some of them attained was considerable. Many of the truths of Christianity seemed fixed in their minds (especially in some instances) so that they would speak to me of them and ask such questions about them as were necessary to render them more plain and clear to their understandings.

The children also and young people who attended the school made considerable proficiency (at least some of them) in their learning, so that had they understood the English language well they would have been able to read somewhat readily in a Psalter.

But that which was most of all desirable and gave me the greatest encouragement amidst many difficulties and disconsolate hours was that the truths of God's Word seemed at times to be attended with some power upon the hearts and consciences of the Indians. And especially this appeared evident in a few instances who were awakened to some sense of their miserable estate by nature and appeared solicitous for deliverance from it. Several of them came of their own accord to discourse with me about their soul's concerns, and some with tears inquired "what they should do to be saved" Acts 16:30, and whether the God that Christians served would be merciful to those that had been frequently drunk, etc.

And although I can't say I have satisfactory evidences of their being "renewed in the spirit of their mind" Ephesians 4:23 and savingly converted to God, yet the Spirit of God did (I apprehend) in such a manner attend the means of grace, and so operate upon their minds thereby as might justly afford matter of encouragement to hope that God designed good to them and that he was preparing his way into their souls.

There likewise appeared a reformation in the lives and manners of the Indians.

Their idolatrous sacrifices (of which there was but one or two that I know of after my coming among them) were wholly laid

<!-- p. 575 -->

aside. And their heathenish custom of dancing, hallowing, etc., they seemed in a considerable measure broken off from. And I could not but hope that they were reformed in some measure from the sin of drunkenness. They likewise manifested a regard to the Lord's Day, and not only behaved soberly themselves, but took care also to keep their children in order.

Yet after all I must confess that as there were many hopeful appearances among them, so there were some things more discouraging. And while I rejoiced to observe any seriousness and concern among them about the affairs of their souls, still I was not without continual fear and concern lest such encouraging appearances might prove like "a morning cloud that passeth away" Hosea 6:4.

When I had spent near a year with the Indians, I informed them that I expected to leave them in the spring then approaching, and to be sent to another tribe of Indians at a great distance from them, upon hearing of which they appeared very sorrowful, and some of them endeavored to persuade me to continue with them, urging that they had now heard so much about their soul's concerns that they could never more be willing to live as they had done without a minister and further instructions in the way to heaven, etc. Whereupon I told them they ought to be willing that others also should hear about their souls' concerns, seeing those needed it as much as themselves. Yet further to dissuade me from going, they added that those Indians to whom I had thoughts of going (as they had heard) were not willing to become Christians, as they were, and therefore urged me to tarry with them. I then told them that they might receive further instruction without me, but the Indians to whom I expected to be sent could not, there being no minister near to teach them. And hereupon I advised them, in case I should leave them and be sent otherwhere, to remove to Stockbridge, where they might be supplied with land and conveniences of living, and be under the ministry of the Rev. Mr. Sergeant; which advice and proposal they seemed disposed to comply with.

On April 6th, 1744, I was ordered and directed by the Correspondents for the Indian mission to take leave of the people with whom I had then spent a full year and to go (as soon as conveniently I could) to a tribe of Indians on Delaware River in Pennsylvania.

<!-- p. 576 -->

These orders I soon attended, and on April 29th took leave of my people, who were mostly removed to Stockbridge under the care of the Rev. Mr. Sergeant. I then set out on my journey toward Delaware, and on May 10th met with a number of Indians in a place called Minissink, about an hundred and forty miles from Kaunaumeek (the place where I spent the last year) and directly in my way to Delaware River. With these Indians I spent some time, and first addressed their King in a friendly manner; and after some discourse and attempts to contract a friendship with him, I told him I had a desire (for his benefit and happiness) to instruct them in Christianity. At which he laughed, turned his back upon me, and went away. I then addressed another principal man in the same manner, who said he was willing to hear me. After some time I followed the King into his house and renewed my discourse to him, but he declined talking and left the affair to another, who appeared to be a rational man. He began and talked very warmly near a quarter of an hour together; he inquired why I desired the Indians to become Christians, seeing the Christians were so much worse than the Indians are in their present state. The Christians, he said, would lie, steal, and drink worse than the Indians. 'Twas they first taught the Indians to be drunk: And they stole from one another to that degree that their rulers were obliged to hang them for it, and that was not sufficient to deter others from the like practice. But the Indians, he added, were none of them ever hanged for stealing, and yet they did not steal half so much; and he supposed that if the Indians should become Christians they would then be as bad as these. And hereupon he said they would live as their fathers lived and go where their fathers were when they died. I then freely owned, lamented, and joined with him in condemning the ill conduct of some who are called Christians: told him these were not Christians in heart, that I hated such wicked practices, and did not desire the Indians to become such as these. And when he appeared calmer I asked him if he was willing that I should come and see them again: He replied he should be willing to see me again as a friend, if I would not desire 'em to become Christians. I then bid them farewell and prosecuted my journey toward Delaware. And May 13th I arrived at a place called by the Indians, Sakhauwotung, within the Forks of Delaware in Pennsylvania.

Here also when I came to the Indians I saluted their King and

<!-- p. 577 -->

others in a manner I thought most engaging, and soon after informed the King of my desire to instruct them in the Christian religion. After he had consulted a few minutes with two or three old men, he told me he was willing to hear. I then preached to those few that were present, who appeared very attentive and well disposed. And the King in particular seemed both to wonder and at the same time to be well pleased with what I taught them respecting the Divine Being, etc. And since that time he has ever shown himself friendly to me, giving me free liberty to preach in his house whenever I think fit. Here therefore I have spent the greater part of the summer past preaching usually in the King's house.

The number of Indians in this place is but small; most of those that formerly belonged here are dispersed and removed to places farther back in the country. There are not more than ten houses hereabouts that continue to be inhabited; and some of these are several miles distant from others, which makes it difficult for the Indians to meet together so frequently as could be desired.

When I first began to preach here the number of my hearers was very small, often not exceeding twenty or twenty-five persons. But towards the latter part of the summer their number increased, so that I have frequently had forty persons or more at once; and oftentimes the most of those belonging to those parts came together to hear me preach.

The effects which the truths of God's Word have had upon some of the Indians in this place are somewhat encouraging. Sundry of them are brought to renounce idolatry and to decline partaking of those feasts which they used to offer in sacrifice to certain supposed unknown powers. And some few instances among them have for a considerable time manifested a serious concern for their souls' eternal welfare, and still continue to "inquire the way to Zion" Jeremiah 50:5 with such diligence, affection, and becoming solicitude as gives me reason to hope that "God who (I trust) has begun this work in them" Philippians 1:6 will carry it on until it shall issue in their saving conversion to himself. These not only detest their old idolatrous notions, but strive also to bring their friends off from them. And as they are seeking salvation for their own souls, so they seem desirous, and some of them take pains, that others might be excited to do the like.

In July last I heard of a number of Indians residing at a place

<!-- p. 578 -->

(called Kauksesauchung) more than thirty miles westward from the place where I usually preach. I visited them, found about thirty persons, and proposed my desire of preaching to them: They readily complied, and I preached to them only twice, they being just then removing from this place (where they only lived for the present) to Susquehanna River where they belonged.

While I was preaching they appeared sober and attentive, and were somewhat surprised, having never before heard of these things. There were two or three who suspected that I had some ill design upon them, and urged that the white people had abused them and taken their lands from them, and therefore they had no reason to think that they were now concerned for their happiness, but on the contrary that they designed to make them slaves or get them on board their vessels and make them fight with the people over the water (as they expressed it) meaning the French and Spaniards. However, the most of them appeared very friendly and told me they were then going directly home to Susquehanna, and desired I would make them a visit there, and manifested a considerable desire of further instruction.

This invitation gave me some encouragement in my great work, and made me hope that God designed to "open an effectual door to me" 1 Corinthians 16:9 for spreading the Gospel among the poor heathen farther westward.

In the beginning of October last, with the advice and direction of the Correspondents for the Indian mission, I undertook a journey to Susquehanna. And after three days tedious travel, two of them through a wilderness almost unpassable by reason of mountains and rocks, and two nights lodging in the open wilderness, I came to an Indian settlement on the side of Susquehanna River, called Opeholhaupung, where were twelve Indian houses and (as nigh as I could learn) about seventy souls old and young belonging to them.

Here also soon after my arrival I visited the King, addressing him with expressions of kindness, and after a few words of friendship informed him of my desire to teach them the knowledge of Christianity. He hesitated not long before he told me that he was willing to hear. I then preached and continued there several days, preaching every day as long as the Indians were at home. And they in order to hear me deferred the design of their general hunting (which they were just then entering upon) for the space of three or four days.

<!-- p. 579 -->

The men, I think, universally (except one) attended my preaching. Only the women, supposing the affair we were upon was of a public nature belonging only to the men, and not what every individual person should concern himself with, could not readily be persuaded to come and hear; but after much pains used with them for that purpose, some few ventured to come and stand at a distance.

When I had preached to the Indians several times, some of them very frankly proposed what they had to object against Christianity; and so gave me a fair opportunity for using my best endeavors to remove from their minds those scruples and jealousies they labored under: And when I had endeavored to answer their objections, some appeared much satisfied. I then asked the King if he was willing I should visit and preach to them again, if I should live to the next spring: He replied he should be heartily willing for his own part, and added he wished the young people would learn, etc. I then put the same question to the rest: Some answered they should be very glad, and none manifested any dislike to it.

There were sundry other things in their behavior, which appeared with a comfortable and encouraging aspect; that upon the whole I could not but rejoice I had taken that journey among them, although it was attended with many difficulties and hardships. The method I used with them and the instructions I gave them (I am persuaded) were means in some measure to remove their heathenish jealousies and prejudices against Christianity: And I could not but hope "the God of all grace" 1 Peter 5:10 was preparing their minds to receive the "truth as it is in Jesus" John 1:17. If this may be the happy consequence, I shall not only rejoice in my past labors and fatigues, but shall, I trust, also be "willing to spend and be spent" 2 Corinthians 12:15 if I may thereby be instrumental "to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God" Acts 26:18.

Thus, Sir, I have given you a faithful account of what has been most considerable respecting my mission among the Indians; in which I have studied all convenient brevity. I shall only now take leave to add a word or two respecting the difficulties that attend the Christianizing of these poor pagans.

In the first place, their minds are filled with prejudices against Christianity, on account of the vicious lives and unchristian behavior of some that are called Christians. These not only set before

<!-- p. 580 -->

them the worst examples, but some of them take pains, expressly in words, to dissuade them from becoming Christians; foreseeing that if these should be converted to God the hope of their unlawful gain would thereby be lost.

Again, these poor heathens are extremely attached to the customs, traditions, and fabulous notions of their fathers. And this one seems to be the foundation of all their other notions, viz., that 'twas not the same God made them who made the white people, but another who commanded them to live by hunting, etc., and not conform to the customs of the white people. Hence when they are desired to become Christians they frequently reply that they will live as their fathers lived and go to their fathers when they die. And if the miracles of Christ and his apostles be mentioned to prove the truth of Christianity, they also mention sundry miracles which their fathers have told them were anciently wrought among the Indians, and which Satan makes them believe were so. They are much attached to idolatry, frequently making feasts, which they eat in honor to some unknown beings, who, they suppose, speak to them in dreams, promising them success in hunting and other affairs, in case they will sacrifice to them. They oftentimes also offer their sacrifices to the spirits of the dead, who, they suppose, stand in need of favors from the living, and yet are in such a state as that they can well reward all the offices of kindness that are shown them. And they impute all their calamities to the neglect of these sacrifices.

Furthermore, they are much awed by those among themselves who are called Powwows, who are supposed to have a power of enchanting, or poisoning them to death, or at least in a very distressing manner. And they apprehend it would be their sad fate to be thus enchanted, in case they should become Christians.

Lastly, the manner of their living is likewise a great disadvantage to the design of their being Christianized. They are almost continually roving from place to place; and 'tis but rare that an opportunity can be had with some of them for their instruction. There is scarce any time of the year wherein the men can be found generally at home, except about six weeks before, and in the season of planting their corn, and about two months in the latter part of summer, from the time they begin to roast their corn until 'tis fit to gather in.

As to the hardships that necessarily attend a mission among

<!-- p. 581 -->

them, the fatigues of frequent journeying in the wilderness, the unpleasantness of a mean and hard way of living, and the great difficulty of addressing "a people of a strange language" Psalms 114:1, these I shall at present pass over in silence; designing what I have already said of difficulties attending this work, not for the discouragement of any, but rather for the incitement of all who love "the appearing and kingdom of Christ" 2 Timothy 4:1 to frequent the throne of grace with earnest supplications that the heathen, who were anciently promised to Christ for his inheritance, may now actually and speedily be brought into his kingdom of grace made heirs of immortal glory.

I am, Sir,

Your obedient, humble servant, David Brainerd.

From the Forks of

Delaware in Pennsylvania,

Nov. 5, 1744

P.S. It should have been observed in the preceding account, that although the number of Indians in the place I visited on Susquehanna River, in October last, is but small, yet their numbers in the adjacent places are very considerable: Who, 'tis hopeful, might be brought to embrace Christianity by the example of others. But being at present somewhat more savage and unacquainted with the English than these I visited, I thought it not best to make my first attempts among them; hoping I might hereafter be better introduced among them by means of these. Sundry of the neighboring settlements are much larger than this; so that there are probably several hundreds of the Indians not many miles distant.

D.B.

#### Brainerd to John Sergeant

Woodbury, March 15, 1745

Reverend and Honored Sir,

In November last, I attempted to send you a line by Mr. Van Schaick, to inform you of the state of affairs with me, and actually wrote; but, he leaving New York an hour sooner than I expected, I was disappointed. And now I am in the greatest hurry, and can but hint at things I would otherwise be a little more particular

<!-- p. 582 -->

in. As to my affairs here, I took a journey last October to Susquehanna, and continued there some time; preaching frequently to the Indians in a place called Opeholhaupung, about fifteen or twenty miles down the river from the place you formerly visited. I supposed I had some encouragement among them, and I propose to visit them again about the middle of next month, with leave of divine Providence, and think to spend most of the summer in those parts, if a door opens for it. There is one peculiar difficulty in the way; the lands these Indians live upon belong to the Six Nations, that is, the Mohawks, and it is something doubtful whether they will suffer a missionary to come among their tributaries, and on their lands. Yet this difficulty, we hope, may be removed by the influence of the Governor of Pennsylvania, who maintains a strict friendship with the Six Nations, whose assistance the Correspondents have endeavored to engage in this affair. May he, who has the hearts of all men in his hands, open their hearts to receive the Gospel.

I have, this winter past, had more encouragement among the Indians of the Delaware than ever before. A spirit of seriousness and concern has seemed to spread among them, and many of them have been very attentive and desirous of instruction. But I have also met with many discouragements, so that I scarcely know what to say. Yet I am not discouraged, but still hope that the day of divine power shall come, when they shall become a willing people.

I long to hear of your affairs; and especially how things are like to turn out with respect to your plan of a free boarding school, which is an affair much upon my heart amidst all my heavy concerns, and I can learn nothing whether it is likely to succeed or not.

I fully designed to have given something considerable for promoting that good design; but whether I shall be able to give anything, or whether it will be my duty to do so under present circumstances, I know not. I have met with sundry losses lately, to the value of sixty or seventy pounds, New England money. In particular, I broke my mare's leg last fall in my journey to Susquehanna, and was obliged to kill her on the road and prosecute my journey on foot, and I can't get her place supplied for fifty pounds. And I have lately moved to have a colleague or companion

<!-- p. 583 -->

with me, for my spirits sink with my solitary circumstances. And I expect to contribute something to his maintenance, seeing his salary must be raised wholly in this country and can't be expected from Scotland.

I sold my teakettle to Mr. Jo. Woodbridge, and an iron kettle to Mr. Timothy Woodbridge, both which amounted to something more than four pounds, which I ordered them to pay to you for the school. I hope you will use the money that way; if not, you are welcome to it for yourself. I desire my teapot and bed ticking may be improved to the same purpose.

As to my blankets, I desired Mr. Woodbridge to take the trouble of turning them into deerskins. If he has not done it, I wish he would, and send the skins to Mr. Hopkins, or, if it might be, to Mr. Bellamy. Please to remember me to Madam and all friends.

I am, Sir, in greatest haste, Your obedient humble servant,

David Brainerd.

#### Brainerd to Eleazer Wheelock

Crossweeksung in N. Jersey,

Dec. 30, 1745

Rev. and Dear Sir,

The large manuscript that accompanies this letter is a copy of a journal I lately sent home to Scotland. And I am apprehensive 'twill not be unwelcome to you. You are sensible, Sir, that I have made some attempts to obtain a colleague, and that I proposed to collect something for his support among religious people in one place and another. Dear Mr. Ebenezer Mills gave me encouragement of gathering something among Christians round about him. And I desired Mr. Barker to ask the same of you and Mr. Williams of Lebanon. And I have since been informed by my friend Sam Rockwell that you not only attempted to subvene something for that purpose but had a prospect of accomplishing what you proposed; so that (as he said) I might look out for the man, as soon as I pleased, to be my companion. This news appeared almost too good to be true, since most men "seek their own" Philippians 2:21; so that 'tis difficult to gather anything for Jesus Christ.

However, I have sent you this journal, hoping 'twill be a means

<!-- p. 584 -->

to animate and encourage Christians to do something toward this good work. And I desire you would make use of it among ministers and people for that purpose in a manner you shall think best. Only I entreat that you would not suffer it or any part of it to be thrown into the press if anybody should be minded so to do.

I doubt not by that time you have read my journal through you'll be more sensible of the need I stand in of a companion in travel than ever you was before.

The pressure of my business is such that I was obliged to employ another hand to transcribe it for me, except the general remarks at the latter end, which I wrote myself: and he has not been careful to preserve the printing and distinct paragraphs as he ought to have been. The former of these difficulties might have been redressed, if I'd had time, but the latter could not. I hope, however, you'll be able to read it. There were some sentences wholly omitted, which I have thrown as addendas into the last page, and have there shown where they ought to be read.

I should be glad, if it might be, that dear Mr. Ebenezer Mills might have the perusal of it for his own comfort, as well as for the furtherance of my proposal and design.

The good work you will find largely treated of in the journal still continues among the Indians, though the astonishing divine influence that has been among them is in considerable measure abated. Yet there are several instances of persons newly awakened and one remarkable instance of saving conversion in the judgment of charity very likely. When I consider the doings of the Lord among these Indians, and then take a view of my journal, I must say 'tis a faint representation I have given of them.

May these papers be blessed of God for the quickening and comfort of all his own people that may read or hear them: and to the awakening and conversion of others.

I entreat, Sir, you would write to me as soon as possible and let me know what prospect there is obtaining what we want among you in those parts. You may enclose your writing to me in a letter to Mr. Pemberton, and only let me know what the letter is about, and he'll freely pay the postage, if you are obliged to send it by the post.

Please to give my duty to Mr. Williams, my respects to your

<!-- p. 585 -->

dear spouse. And if you can let my brother Mason hear from me by means of these papers I should be glad, for I han't time to write to him. I enjoy more health than I would expect amidst sermons, labors, cares, and fatigues, but am not healthy. I hope you will not forget to pray for

your unworthy fellow laborer and humble servant

David Brainerd

#### Brainerd to William Bradford

Princeton N. Jersey Sept. 20, 1746

Dear Sir,

When I first began to write that which I now call "Appendix to the *Journal*," I had no thoughts of its being so large, nor of so particularly distinguishing it from the *Journal* by the name of an "Appendix:" and therefore made an Introduction accordingly, by saying I should not conclude the present *Journal*, but that etc., calling it virtually a part of the *Journal*; but as I have made it a distinct Appendix in the title page I entreat you to begin it there. I should have concluded what I had at present to offer upon the affairs, respecting my mission, with the preceding account of the money collected and expended for the religious interest of the Indians, but that, etc.

And seeing you have not as yet printed the title page of the first part of the *Journal*, I desire that you would be allowed to transpose the two first texts of Scripture there quoted, i.e., let that in the Isaiah 55 of Isaiah and Isaiah 55:13 verse stand first, and let that in the Isaiah 65 and Isaiah 65:1 second.

I likewise desire that instead of the last passage of Scripture quoted in the title page of the second part of the *Journal*, viz., Psalms 110:3, you would be pleased to insert therein Psalms 118:23. This is the Lord saying, it is marvelous in our eyes.

As the first particular here mentioned, viz., the beginning of the Appendix, is of some considerable importance, so I trust you will take special care that it ben't neglected.

I am, Sir,

Your obedient humble servant, David Brainerd

<!-- p. 586 -->

#### John Brainerd to Ebenezer Pemberton

For the Rev. Mr. Ebenezer Pemberton at New York.

Since you are pleased to require me to give an account of the present situation of affairs among those Indians which, at this present time, I have the more immediate care of, I shall endeavor to do it in as brief but just a manner as I can. And, 1st. There are now belonging to the society of Indians something upward of one hundred and sixty persons, old and young, who, I think, may properly be called inhabitants of the town. 2dly. Among these there are thirty-seven who have been admitted to the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper, and who, in a judgment of charity, appear to have experienced a work of saving grace in their hearts. There are also several others who, as I have reason to think, are truly religious and stand as proper candidates for those Gospel ordinances.

3dly. Out of the number first mentioned there are about thirty persons who came to this place since my arrival here, which was the 15th of April last. About ten of these are adults. I have reason to think all rationally convinced of the truth of the Christian religion, and under some degree of concern; and most of 'em appear to be much concerned, and their convictions seem to be permanent and genuine.

The next thing I shall mention is the school, which consists of fifty-three children who properly belong to it and generally attend upon it; twenty-seven of these read in the Testament, and most of 'em can say the Assembly's shorter catechism throughout by heart. Others read in Psalters, spelling books, and primers, and many of 'em can say the catechism half through. These children are many of 'em under religious impressions, and seem to be earnestly inquiring the way to Zion; and some, even of the newcomers, are much concerned for the salvation of their souls, and all that are grown to any considerable bigness (so far as we can know by observing and inquiring of their parents, and of one concerning another) do live in the constant performance of secret duties.

As touching their secular affairs, they are much more comfortable than they were. They have upwards of forty acres of English grain in the ground, and near about so much Indian corn; and they do, I think, in general follow their secular business as

<!-- p. 587 -->

well as can be expected, considering they have all their days been used to sloth and idleness. Thus, Sir, I have given a very brief answer to your demands, but, I think, just account of the present condition of these Indians; and am,

Rev. Sir, yours, etc., John Brainerd.

From Bethel, the Indian Town in New Jersey, June 23, 1747

#### Edwards to John Brainerd

Northampton Decem. 14, 1747

Dear Sir,

I have read through your deceased brother's papers, containing his Life, and have determined to publish an abstract of them. I have with this sent to you a letter to Gov. Belcher, desiring his leave to dedicate the book to him; which I desire you to wait on his excellency with. If he should consent to have the book dedicated to him, it might not only tend to make it the more taken notice of, and so the more useful, but also may do honor to your brother's memory, whom many in his lifetime strove to lay under disgrace. I have sent my letter to the Governor open, that you may see it, but desire you handsomely to seal and deliver it.

In writing your brother's Life it will be unavoidable but that mention must be made of your brother's expulsion from the College: and therefore I think it is necessary that a just and particular account be given of that matter, so that I should be glad that when you come hither in the spring, you would come furnished to give me a just, exact, and certain account of that affair, that the Rector may have no cause, nor find any reason to complain of the least misrepresentation in my respect. I should be glad also to know particularly what offer your brother made to the Rector from time to time of satisfaction, in order to his being restored to College. There is mention made in his private journals of his making attempts to be reconciled several times, one in June and another in July, 1743, and particularly I think I have heard him speak of a confession he offered (or something of that nature) to the justice, at Hartford, the May after his expulsion, at the time of the election, but there is no account what it was. There is included in his diary a copy of the confession he offered at last, at the time of that commencement that his class took their degrees,

<!-- p. 588 -->

but no other. Perhaps Mr. Burr may be able to give a particular justification of some of these matters, and Mr. Mills. I should be glad that when you are on your journey hither you would inquire of him, or any other that you think would be likely to inform. I think your brother told me that the Rector acknowledged that the confession he offered at last was Christian satisfaction. However, I would be glad to be more fully informed of that matter.

I want also to be more particularly informed of some things in your brother's life: something more particular concerning his parentage, his mother in particular, who she was and whence descended: and if there was anything remarkable in her childhood, any remarkable danger and deliverance, or restoration, or any other thing worthy to be noted in writing his life: a particular account of his mission to the Indians; how the Society in Scotland came first to appoint a number of commissioners in New York and the Jerseys; how the commissioners came to hear of and improve employ Mr. Brainerd; how they came first to send him to Kaunaumeek; how he came afterwards to be called thence and sent to the Forks of Delaware. And perhaps Mr. Tennent and some others that were well acquainted with him may be able to inform of some remarkable things of him, of his character, behavior, or speeches that may be worthy to be inserted in his Life. And I want to be more particularly informed of your brother's illness last winter at Mr. Dickinson's, for there his Journal is very short. I want also to be informed whether your brother's public *Journal* be continued till he left the Indians, or whether anything further was published by him or prepared for the press beyond what was printed at Philadelphia. If there was, I should be glad to see it, that I mayn't publish the same thing over again out of his diary. I should be glad that you would bring me an account of these things when you come in the spring. And also bring any other of your brother's papers that may contain what may be worthy to be inserted. Some of his letters to his friends that I have seen are remarkable, and well worth publishing, and I doubt not but they were among others that were, that I have not yet seen: I desire that you would bring some of them, such as you think are most worthy to be taken notice of, to yourself or others; and particularly I desire you would as you come along, in my name request of Esther Sherman that she would send me

<!-- p. 589 -->

some of his letters to her. Your brother in his diary often mentions her writing on divine subjects, and I perceive he spent abundance of time in writing; I don't know how to think that all that he meant was writing sermons: I would be glad to see some of these his composing on diverse subjects.

On further considering your brother's diary, since I wrote the preceding part of this letter, I find that I want to be informed of some further particulars, in order to writing his Life, which probably Mr. Pemberton or Mr. Burr can give information in. There is mention made of a meeting of ministers that examined him at New York, in Novem, 1742. I want to know what meeting of ministers that was; whether a meeting of the Presbytery, or of the commissioners; why the commissioners gave him so long a space, after he was examined at New York concerning his qualifications for the mission, before they actually sent him on the business, as from Novem to the next April; whether it was because they looked on the winter season unfit to engage in such business.

It seems by your brother's diary, that when he was examined at the time forementioned, the design was that he should be sent to the Indians in Pennsylvania, unreadable to have that expectation all winter, of going to those Indians. I would be informed how the Correspondents came to change their minds, and when the spring came sent him to Kaunaumeek; what your brother's special business to N. York and the Jerseys was when, the next spring, he went thither from E. Hampton before he went to Kaunaumeek, and what meeting of ministers that was that he at that time met at Woodbridge; whether a meeting of the Presbytery or of the Correspondents, and what instructions he there received.

He took three journeys from Kaunaumeek to N. York and the Jerseys; one in May, 1743, another in September following, when he went no further than N. York; another at the latter end of March, the next year. I want to know what was the special occasion of these journeys, who his interpreter was at Kaunaumeek, an Englishman or Indian, what encouragement the commissioners saw in the state of the Delaware Indians that unreadable them to send a missionary to them rather than any other Indians.

I suppose my funeral sermon on your brother is by this time printed. Mr. Bromfield writes me word, in a letter dated Decem.

<!-- p. 590 -->

1, that it was then in the press and would be finished in about 10 days from that time, and that Maj. Henchman had agreed to print it without any subscription and to send me my part of them, and also that he with some other gentlemen had determined to send a number of them as a present to you.——I am Sir,

Your affectionate friend Jonath. Edwards

P.S. If I had received one of my sermons on your brother's funeral, I would now send one to Gov. Belcher. If he consents that I should dedicate his Life to him, it may not be unreadable for you to make a present of one of yours to him, when you receive them.
